colleague the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals might be taken into account. It seems that hon. gentlemen do not want all the Estimates to go through until they have been given certain information they desire, but I see no reason why some of these items should not be taken up and discussed and perhaps passed. There is no particular objection to holding an item or two for a general discussion and for eliciting any information that is desired; but at this time of the session, when we want to get all the business done as rapidly as possible, I think there is some force in the suggestion of my colleague that we should go on with some of these items.

Ordinarily that would
be the part of wisdom. The difficulty is that to these items, which are all large, there will probably be added other items, in the way of Bills, either providing for the expenditure of large amounts of money or increasing the obligations of the country to railway enterprises of more or less significance. If this were an ordinary
4 p.m. case I should have no objection at all to getting rid of some of these small items; but the point is this. The press tells us that these items will be augmented very materially, and, until we know what these further items are to be, I do not think we should be asked to vote these large amounts. I would suggest that the acting minister tell the House now
ft

what other railway legislation is to be brought down which will further obligate the country. That information may bear on the discussion of the items before us, many of which are large, such as the Hudson Bay railway, the National Transcontinental, and the Welland canal. If we are to undertake other large expenditures in addition to these, it is only fair that the House should know what they aTe going to be. We are a little dubious as to what may happen. The Government has seen fit to slip in a subsidy amongst the ordinary Estimates, which is establishing a precedent. Hon. gentlemen know that subsidies are invariably brought down in what is know as a Subsidy Bill-separate altogether from the Estimates. Each item is discussed on its merits, if the House sees fit, and a separate Act is passed. A year ago the Government assured a lot of applicants that no Subsidy Bill would be brought down; but here, in the Estimates, not in a Subsidy Bill, they are providing for the payment of a subsidy of $384,000. ' If this practice is to be followed, a dozen subsidies could be placed in the Estimates. Under the circumstances, then, I think it would be wise for the Government to put their cards on the table and tell us what they propose to do in the way of aid to railways. We shall then be prepared to discuss intelligently the items before us, and perhaps we may have to cut some of them down if the other expenditures are to be large. I repeat that this is not an ordinary case of taking up the items one by one, and allowing one or two to stand/ on which all the information can be given. If we pass all the other items, the information as to these subsidies will not help us out of the difficulty,
There is force in some parts of what my hon. .friend says, while in other parts there is not quite so much force, if he will allow me to- say so.
There is a great deal of force.
Item 110 introduces a new principle, that is, voting a subsidy as a 'Supplementary Estimate.
That was not my point. My point was that the Government may bring in half a dozen subsidies as Supplementary Estimates.
If they do they cannot surprise you with them, as they will be brought down in the regular way.
In an irregular way.

There are, however, a number of items, which, whether others are brought in or not, have, to put it mildly, to be passed, because the work must go on. For instance, with reference to the Prince Edward Island railway, there are items for strengthening bridges, original construction, surveys and inspections, increase of accommodation and facilities, also a small amount to provide for the car ferry. That is an old matter, and this vote is to carry to completion and to operate what has already been agreed upon by both sides of the House. Then there is an item to bring the New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island railway line up to Intercolonial railway branch line standard.
We passed that the other night.
Then there is the item to bring the International line up to the Intercolonial branch line standard.
We have already passed a number of the items which my hon. friend has mentioned. These are yet to be passed: numbers 103, 106, 107, 108, 109, 110, 118, 120, 123.

The different items in item 103 are all ordinary items for carrying out a policy which has already been agreed upon in reference to the car ferry. Item No. 106, the Hudson Bay railway, is also an old subject. That item is to carry out what has been under progress for a considerable length of time, and the work must be proceeded with, I suppose, unless the House comes, to the conclusion that we are to stop operations on that road. The same is true of item No. 107, National Transcontinental railway.
My hon. friend, it he keeps on, will make out too strong a case.
I thought the Transcontinental was completed a long time ago.

Unless my hon. friend, wishes to push the matter as far as not to allow anything to pass, because he is afraid that something else may be put in the Supplementary Estimates-which is not very brave .of my hon. friend-I think we should make some progress with these items.

The Minister of Trade and Commerce is not putting the matter quite rightly. I did not say " for fear that

something may be put in the Supplementary Estimates." I said that that could be done. There are yet to come before the House three railway measures asking for aid.
Are you sure of that?
The Government press will have to be muzzled if that is not true.
That will be a hard operation.
That announcement by the Minister of Public Works will send the stocks down to-morrow.

In the hope and full confidence that that additional legislation, will be introduced, several things are taking place every day. The chief point that I raised was this: we shall be here only a short time, we all hope. We ought, therefore, to know now what the railway legislation is to be, particularly that part of it which will put the country under further obligation. If it were early in the session that these Estimates were up, it would be a different matter, but there carmot be more than a few days between the passage of these items and the introduction of that railway legislation. The Government, therefore,
[DOT] ought to give us an idea of their programme in reference to railway legislation so that the members will know what they are asked to vote for railway purposes including the Estimates. I would suggest that we discuss this Prince Edward Island railway item for a little while, and then perhaps the Government will be in a position to give us their programme in regard to railway legislation.

Last fall it was announced that the Government had made a rate of six cents per bushel, or ten cents per cwt. on grain shipped all-rail from Armstrong to the East. So far as I know, no statement has yet been made in regard to that, just as no statement has yet been made in regard to the commandeering of wheat, anxiously as we have been looking for it. We would be pleased to have a statement from the minister as to the policy and how it worked out.

I explained that matter the other evening in the hon. member's absence, but I will do so again. The Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) made a rate of six cents from Armstrong to Montreal and Quebec during' the season while

navigation was closed, and so far as the Transcontinental is concerned that rate is still being kept in force between Armstrong and Quebec. A quantity of grain has been carried over the Transcontinental during the season between the closing of navigation and the opening.
What was the reason for giving that special rate?

It was in order to relieve
the congestion in the West by taking the grain East. There was a very large crop, and the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur were filled.
Did it relieve the situation?	.

Eight million bushels were
carried over the Transcontinental.
That is a mere bagatelle.

I think it was quite a help
tc take out 8,000,000 bushels. I do not know whether the member from the West will agree with my hon. friend.

Where did the grain
go to?
To Quebec, St. John, Halifax and Montreal. Some was shipped through to St. John for export.
Via Quebec?
Yes.	[DOT]
How much?
I cannot tell off-hand.

Approximately? That
is a very important matter.

I can get the figures. I
know there was grain shipped to the elevator at Quebec for 'Storage until the opening of navigation.

What is its storage
capacity?

One million five hundred
thousand bushels. Some went to Halifax for export, and of course a lot went to Montreal for export.
What went to Montreal does not concern us, because it would not go by the Government road.
All the ports were congested.

How much grain went to Halifax and how much to St. John for

305P
-export? What route did it go by, and what was the rate from Winnipeg to the shipping point?
Did six cents carry it to the seaport? If not, how much did it cost to carry the wheat from Winnipeg to the seaport? Can the minister state now what that rate was?

I have not these rates before me. But six cents is the summer Tate to Montreal, and that rate would be added to if the grain had to be sent to Portland, St. John, or Halifax. But the six-cent rate must have been quite a help, I should think, because it mean that they got the summer rate from the closing to the opening of navigation. The rate from Winnipeg to Armstrong is similar to that from Winnipeg to Fort William.
Yes.

The hon. gentleman will see that this was equalizing the rate between Winnipeg and Montreal. The six-cent rate would be practically the same as that *by rail to Port Arthur and thence by vessel to Montreal, and thus it should have been a great advantage to those who were able to ship during the winter season.

Is it not true that there is really no elevator system to speak of in [DOT]connection with the Government system of railways? The elevator at St. John was burned down two years ago, and not a step has been taken to rebuild it. St. John formerly had good elevator accommodation. There is no elevator accommodation whatever in connection with the Transcontinental. So, while the rate was given to Quebec, there was no encouragement to shippers, no facilities were provided for handling the grain at the seaport. The result is that little advantage was taken *of the rate. The minister speaks of eight million bushels as though it were a large quantity. With proper elevator accommodation and train service the Transcontinental ought to have carried ten times as much. Why, there is over ten million bushels of wheat, on the Goose Lake Branch of the Canadian Northern alone, hung up during the season to the very great loss of the farmers. Yet, 'the minister talks about eight millions [DOT]as a large quantity to be carried over the Transcontinental, one of the finest railways in the world-at least it is one of the finest so far as it was carried out under ithe auspices of the late Government. If
the Government had got to work at the proper time, had rebuilt the St. John elevator, and had enlarged the elevator accommodation at Halifax and Quebec, the Transcontinental might have been made a real factor in the transportation situation. Surely, before these Estimates pass, the Government ought to give an explanation of their want of activity, their want of foresight, their want of attention to the necessities of the case. I think the suggestion of the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) is one that ought to be acted upon. The Minister of Railways coming before this Parliament is like a board of directors coming to consult the shareholders-we representatives of the people are here on behalf of those who have to bear the burdens. The minister tells us: I want you to vote $19,000,000 for various woTks to be carried on. The people, through their representatives in this Parliament, say to the Government: When you are asking for these vast amounts of money you ought to show your hand, you ought to lay your cards upon the table, and let us know what further obligations you are going to ask us during the present session to bear. The hon. member for South Renfrew says that the rumour is widespread and the statements made are specific and positive. And to enforce what he said, I saw the statement to-day in the Toronto News. If there is a newspaper in Canada that is close to this 'Government, that finds a resting place in the very bosom of many prominent members, it is the Toronto News. I believe the editor of that newspaper enjoys with reference to this Government a stronger position than Colonel Allison enjoyed with the Minister of Militia. The editor of the News is the guide, philosopher, friend and adviser of this Government.
Sir 'GEORGE FOSTER: And biographer?
He wrote biography in the days before sin had spread scf widely over this country and before,many good men had been led astray, the editor of the Toronto News among them.
What about yourself?
My hon. friend knows all sides.

I will tell my hon.
friend something about that. I was once a Conservative; but it was a long time ago. My hon. friend knows that there was then the same inactivity with regard to transportation, the same want of attention to

the maritime ports as there is unfortunately to-day; so that many good Conservatives fell away from my hon. friend. Much as they like him personally, yet politically they could not quite stand him, because he did not seem to have that regard for the interests of the country that he should have had. It was about that time too that I took to reading my Bible very carefully. I found that in the old biblical times there were two parties', there was the Liberal party and the party that stood in the place of the Tories of the present day. They were called churls at that time. And I found that the Liberals, even in those old days, had a reputation and enjoyed a popularity for their virtue which has remained with them even down to the present time. I am sorry to see that the party of my hon. friend, the party opposed to the Liberals are not given a very good, character in the Bible. I have great faith in the good book. I recommend my hon. friend to read it. If he likes, I will call his attention to passages which he will find particularly interesting.
The hon. gentleman might quote, just as a test of his knowledge.

I would ask the Acting Minister of Railways why it is that although the Government elevator at St. John was burned down at least two years ago, no steps have been taken to rebuild it. To my mind, it appears inexplicable, especially in view of the fact that, immediately on the outbreak of the war, the Government urged upon the farmers of the West the need of increased production, and, to that end, the planting of more land in grain. Of course, that implied an undertaking on the part of the Government that, so far as it was concerned, it would do everything possible to have the grain sent forward as cheaply and expeditiously as possible and would afford every facility foT transportation.
It strikes me as very inexcusable that the Government should allow that important plant in 'Connection with the Government railway system to remain unbuilt. I should like to know, also, why the Government took no steps to provide elevator accommodation in connection with the Transcontinental railway. The other day the acting minister stated that the Transcontinental was completed away back in September, 1914, even though it was only partially completed. By some peculiar process of
[Mr. Pugslev.l
reasoning the minister seems to think that a railway-or house, I suppose, or Store- might be completed when it was only partially completed. However, that was the view the Government took, and from that time to the present they have provided no elevator accommodation in connection with the Transcontinental railway. I think the minister ought to explain that. In view of the fact that the minister is unable to deny the rumours that are being circulated in the press that Parliament will be called upon to assume further obligations on behalf of the people, he ought, as would be the.act of a prudent minister, to say to us: We will not ask you to pass these items just now. We will wait until we can lay before you all the obligations which you shall be called upon to assume on behalf of the people, and we will ask you to consider with us whether we shall have the means, through direct and' indirect taxes and other sources of revenue, to provide for these other burdens, as well as all the amounts which are included in these Estimates; we will consider the whole matter carefully and in the best interests of the people. Does the minister not see what madness it would be for us to vote $19,000,000 if next week we shall be called upon to assume on behalf of the people obligations amounting to $20,000,000, or $30,000,000, or $40,000,000 in respect to other railway companies? It seems to me that the suggestion of the hon. member for South Renfrew- the suggestion of a prudent member of Parliament, who represents some of the people who. arS to bear these burdens-is reasonable and should be adopted. I should be glad if the minister will explain why the elevator accommodation has not been replaced upon the Intercolonial, and why it has not been enlarged in view of the necessity of providing for increased transportation of grain; also, why no elevator has been provided in connection with the Transcontinental?

In reference to the question asked by the member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles), may I ask the minister how the Government came to undertake to secure this low rate for carrying wheat? Were they requested to do so by any set of men or bv any association? T would ask also if they have carried all or nearly all the grain that has been offered in connection with this low rate to Quebec?

The arrangement to v\hich the hon. gentleman refers was made by the

hon. Mi lister of Railways himself. As I understand it, it was repres'ented to him that there was such a large crop that the Fort William and Port Arthur elevators would not be able to hold all the grain that the railways could carry to them. It was shown to him that the lake-and-rail rate from Port Arthur to Montreal was about 6 cents a bushel, and he was asked if he could not put that rate in force, say from Armstrong, which would be practically the same point as Port Arthur or Fort William, during the winter season, and thus relieve the congestion in the West as much as possible. He put that rate in force, and relieved the situation to the extent of about
8,000,000 bushels of grain that were carried. More grain might have been carried if we had had fuller equipment. Taking the rail-way^over on the 1st of July without any equipment whatever-no engines, no cars, nothing at all to operate the railway-we were forced to take some seventy-five engines off the Intercolonial and as many cars as we could spare in order to operate the line between Winnipeg and the Bast. With the small facilities that we had, we could not do any more than we have done. There is no doubt that many requests came from the West for operation of the Transcontinental to as great an extent as possible, in order that the grain might be carried over that line, thus relieving the situation in the West.
Has any effort been made to get the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific railway to give similar rates?

I cannot say that. The Minister of Railways made the arrangements. I will find that out, though, and let the hon. member know at the next sitting. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) asked a question regarding the elevator at St. John. The elevator that we had there was burned down. We all realize, of course, that that elevator was not of a sufficient capacity for the Government railway system at that port.
Was it not of the same capacity as the elevator at Halifax?

Yes, but I mean for the
future.

The capacity was about
750,000	bushels.

I understand it is the intention to have a very much larger elevator located on Courtenay bay. Of course, that
is in connection with the Public Works Department, and I do not know exactly what the conditions are.

I should like to correct the minister, if he will allow me. Mr. Gute-lius, General Manager of the Intercolonial railway, has said that the elevator will be built, not upon Courtenay bay but in the vicinity of the sugar refinery.
I understand that the elevator is to be built near the sugar refinery out on the point.
That is not on Courtenay bay.

The trackage that is necessary in connection with Courtenay bay is really a part of the elevator scheme. I realize that it is absolutely necessary to have an elevator there. It is necessary to have an elevator in the western section, near Winnipeg or Transcona. This fire, however, occurred since the war started, and we have had a great deal of difficulty so far as finances are concerned. At any rate, expenditures are so large that if we have been able to hold off anything for a short time we have tried to do so. The hon. member for St. John has been complaining very seriously about expenditures that we are making-expenditures that we cannot stop; at St. John he wishes us to make a very large expenditure.
That elevator was burned down before the war began.

I think it was after the outbreak of war. It may have been just about that time. I have urged strongly that the elevator at St. John be constructed as soon as possible. We also require an elevator in the neighbourhood of Transcona, so that the grain can be weighed and inspected at that point instead of being taken during the winter months to Fort William and Port Arthur before being passed on to Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax. These elevators must be built. We must have elevators at St. John and Halifax with very large capacities in order to meet the demands during the winter months.
That is what the people there have been thinking for the last two years.

I cannot understand why the hon. member for St. John should object to work being done at any other point. He wants it all done at St. John. He will vote

for millions to 'be expended bn Courtenay bay or in the building of elevators at St. John, but objects to one dollar being spent in Montreal or at any other place.

My hon. friend must take that back. The statement he has made is absolutely wrong, and absolutely untrue. I do not say that it was deliberate; the Acting Minister of Railways would never be guilty of a deliberate untruth. But the trouble with him is the extraordinary forgetfulness from which he suffers. Does he not Temember that at the last session of Parliament I almost took my political life in my hands, so far as St. John was concerned, when I stated that I would favour cutting the appropriations in half. The cutting down was done all round, and when the Minister of Public Works asked me if I would consent to the appropriations for St. John being cut in half, I said that I would, and I was attacked most bitterly by the Conservative newspapers in St. John for my statement at that time. I have never hesitated to vote for all needed appropriations for other parts of the country, and while I am not afraid to stand up for my own constituency and demand justice, I have always tried to be fair. I would not regard the grain elevator at St. John as a new work at all. The old elevator was part of the equipment or plant connected with the Government system of railways. It was a necessary adjunct of the railway, and a necessary part of its plant. That elevator was burned *down upwards of two years ago, I think; I am quite sure it was before the war broke out. But a new elevator would not be a new work in the sense in which we speak <of hundreds of new works provided for in these Estimates. It would be a case of merely restoring a portion of the plant of the Government railway system which had been destroyed by fire. Tne rebuilding of that elevator is just as necessary in the interests oj: western Canada as it is in the interests of the port of St. John. There are elevators in connection with the Canadian Pacific railway at the port of St. John which are not entirely in the interests of, or for the benefit of, St. John. If we did not have elevators there, either the grain from the West would not be shipped at all, or it would be shipped in the winter season wholly from American ports. I am sorry to say that a vast deal of the western grain is being shipped at the present time from American ports, but, if it were not for the

elevators of the Canadian Pacific railway, it would likely all go that way. The acting minister said that I ask for millions and millions of dollars for St. John. I have never done so. I remember that when the minister came to St. John, shortly after he took office, he tried to make the people believe that I had been very sparing in making appropriations for St. John, that I was not treating St. John well at all. At a banquet which was given to my hon. friend the Minister of Customs and the Minister of Public Works, my hon. friend will remember he was called upon to make a speech, and he said that he had had an opportunity of visiting Courtenay bay, that he was much impressed with the wonderful possibilities of a great harbour there. He said:	" Pugsley has provided, so far as I
can see, for only eighteen or twenty docks; now, gentlemen, I want you to understand that if you are of opinion that he has not provided docks on a sufficiently large scale, all you have to do is to come to me. as Minister of Customs, and I will enlarge this undertaking, and you can rely upon getting millions upon millions of dollars provided out of the overflowing revenues of the country." I merely wish to put my hon. friend right. I am sure he will be the first to apologize for the very unfair remarks which he made with reference to me.

It seems to me that
there is some sort of an arrangement by which the motive originally underlying this discussion should be lost sight of. We had first of all a reference which I did not quite understand by the member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). He suggested that the cards be put on the table. What kind of game is he proposing to play? Then we had hardly got through with that very doubtful suggestion when another hon. gentleman suggested that the Liberal party was speaking from the loins of Judas Iscariot, or made some such Scriptural reference as that. These things, howeveT, did not suffice to obscure the illusion which both the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) made, namely, that they did not wish to express their opinion on this $19,000,000 item because they wished to keep it fresh for the $20,000,000, $30,000,000, or $40,000,000 subsidies that they believe are to be brought down later on. That is, they must be quite willing to grant some of the subsidies which they pretend to object to, because they do not want to impair

the present item in the event of their being brought down; otherwise, there is no sense in their references at all. They would give the impression to the country that they are strongly opposed to any money being paid to any of those other undertakings. They back up into position, giving the people the impression that they are facing one way when as a matter of fact they are going another way. But I go further, I strongly object to giving those roads another dollar. I have objected all along, and I object now; and I know that the people object.	As for the Conservative journals, especially the Toronto News, it is diametrically opposed to giving any of those roads another cent, let alone another dollar. I think it should be well understood that this is the opinion of the country. But I thins: the situation is dangerous, and therefore I have ventured to protest. I think it extremely dangerous that the hen. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) should say that in the event of this $.19,006,900 item being reserved, he wound be ready and willing to undertake the consideration of a $20,000,000, $30,000,000 ot $40,000,000 subsidy. There is something wrong somewhere.

The hon. member for
St. John did not happen to say that.

I think the hon.
gentleman will find that he did say so; otherwise why did he mention $20,000,000, $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 at all?

Does my hon. friend
want an answer?
Yes.

What I said was this:
if the Government intends to come down with a proposition to impose upon the people an obligation of $20,000,000, $30,000,000 or $40,000,000, this item should stand so that the whole matter can be considered, having reference to the resources of the people and their ability to pay.

Precisely so. What I say is that this matter should not be considered at all. The hon. gentleman is prepared to consider it. That is exactly the statement I am making: I am not prepared to consider it. The farmers whom I represent-and I am partly a farmer myself-[DOT] are not so green as not to see through this veiled reference, this pretendjing to take a stand and then backing up into position so. that the hon. gentlemen will be ready
to be convinced at the last moment and be overawed by the Government majority, after they have put up-and I say it without disrespect-a fake opposition. I am opposed to it.

My hon. friend says that he is opposed, to any further assistance to either of these railways; but if the Government comes down and proposes to give them assistance my hon. friend will back it up just as every other 'hon. gentleman on the other side of the House will.

I did not do so before;
I walked out.

My hon. friend was talking about backing up to a position, He backs out of a position altogether. I cannot see that he is half as courageous as his colleagues. His colleagues stay in the House and support the Government that they were elected to support, right or wrong, but my hon. friend) gets out of the difficulty by walking out of the House.
If he gets out of the difficulty what is the matter with that?

What I rose for was to ask the minister if the rate of 6 cents a bushel that the Transcontinental railway gives from Armstrong to Montreal or Quebec is going to be continued in force during the summer as well as during the winter? I would also like to know whether theTe was a profit or loss to the railway in carrying wheat at 6 cents a bushel from Armstrong to Montreal or Quebec. I have always understood that that rate would give a very handsome profit on a road constructed like the National Transcontinental railway, with good grades, upon which one engine could take sixty cars loaded with 1,100 bushels each, or about 65,000 bushels, and haul them from Armstrong down to Quebec. I would like to know if the railway made a profit or a loss for the Government.
Does the hon. gentleman know what the distance is from Armstrong to Quebec?
Yes; about 950 miles.

There was no profit in it; in fact, there was a loss when the wheat was taken to Montreal, for the reason that there were three railways that had to get a portion of the six cents; there was the Transcontinental, the Temiskaming and Northern Ontario, and the Grand Trunk

from North Bay to Montreal. You can see that if you have to divide that rate up, it makes a very small portion for each railway. We can carry grain from Armstrong to Quebec at a profit, but we cannot do so when the grain has to be hauled over three railways. I think we probably made a little out of taking the grain to Quebec.

I am very glad to hear that grain, at 6 cents a bushel, can be carried from Armstrong to Quebec at a profit. I would expect that to be the case, because the,object for which the railway was built was to carry grain out of the western country. What was the through rate during the winter from Armstrong to tidewater .at St. John or Halifax? My understanding is that although the Government gave a rate of 6 cents a bushel from Armstrong to Quebec or Montreal, the through rate over the Transcontinental railway from Winnipeg to St. John was exactly equal to the old Canadian Pacific rate from Winnipeg to St. John, and that, instead of there being a lower rate, instead of it being something good for the people of the West and of Canada, it was nothing more or less than a fake rate arrived at by charging lees on one portion of the Government road and charging more on the balance of the Government road.
You mean that it was a gold brick?

It was a gold brick, nothing more or less, and it gave no outlet for the wheat. The only advantage that there might be in it was the storage that might be secured in Montreal or Quebec. It was generally understood that when the Government gave this rate they were giving something that would be of advantage to the people of Canada. But when they fixed a rate of 6 cents a bushel for 950 or 1,000 miles, and then added to the rate for the balance of the journey so as to bring it up to the old Canadian Pacific rate and so that there should be no competition whatever, how much good were they doing to the people of Canada? That is the information I have, and I believe it is correct.

I would like the hon. member to give me his authority for that statement. There is a through summer rate on the Canadian Pacific, lake and rail, from Winnipeg to St. John. It goes by Port Arthur or Fort William, then by water and rail to St. John.
What is that summer rate?

I cannot give the exact rate. The rate from Winnipeg to Port Arthur and Fort William is the same as the Tate from Winnipeg to Armstrong. Then, from Armstrong to Montreal and Quebec the rate is 6 cents, the same as the summer lake-and-rail rate. When the grain reaches Armstrong on the Transcontinental, it takes the 6-cent rate and goes to Quebec and then on to St. John at the same rate as they carry over the Canadian Pacific in the summer time, that is, the summer rate from Winnipeg to St. John, lake and rail.

I understand that perfectly well. If the Government, on the Transcontinental, can carry grain from Armstrong to Quebec for six cents a bushel at a profit, why cannot they carry it at the same proportionate rate from Quebec to St. John? That seems to be reasonable. That is the only advantage that the people of Canada can obtain. There is no object in cutting down the rate on 1,000 miles of the road and doubling it up on the remaining portion. If you can carry grain at a profit, with a rate of 6 cents a bushel, for the distance between Armstrong and Quebec, surely you ought to make a better profit if you carry it down to St. John at the same proportionate rate per mile, *because you will not have the stoppages' and all the loss incidental to stoppages. My hon. friend said a moment ago that the equipment allowed them to handle only
8,000,000 bushels, and he spoke as if 8,000,000 was a very considerable amount of wheat. In some ways it is, but it is only one-fortieth part, or 2J per cent of last year's crop. What was this road built for? What has the Government been doing when, after four years when the grain is there and cannot be taken out in any other way, when the business is offering and the Government road could carry it at a profit, as the minister says-what has the Government been doing in those four years that their equipment is only capable of handling 8,000,000 bushels during the winter season? My hon. friend has a great deal of explanation ahead of him to convince the people of Canada that the Government has been dealing fairly with the National Transcontinental. Here was the business offering, here was the wheat in danger of being lost-and a great deal of it has been lost for lack of storage capacity in the West-and here was the National Transcontinental, a first-class road,

built at large expense;. here was tide-water at St. John and Halifax; and, according to the minister, the grain could be carried at a profit by the railway. But the grain has not been carried; the farmers have not been relieved; they have lost tens of thousands of bushels of grain; and the Government comes forward and says they are able to carry only 8,000,000 bushels. Surely the minister has some better explanation than that, because that is no explanation at all. Let me draw my hon. friend's attention and the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce to another thing-something that the Minister of Trade and Commerce might have done when he commandeered the
16,000,000 bushels of wheat. Some time towards the end of last October I was out West in the town of Estevan, in my constituency. The men on the market there were quoting 93 or 94 cents, I forget which, for wheat on the track; that is, a farmer could get 93 or 94 cents if he was able to get a car and loaded it up. If he could not get a car and could not get the wheat on the track, he could only get 83 or 84 cents a bushel, or exactly 10 cents a bushel less than what the wheat brought on the track. The wheat buyer is not to blame for this. If he buys wheat toward the end of October and is unable to get a car, he puts the grain in his elevator, and has to figure on storage, insurance of the wheat, and interest on the cost until the following May. That means that he, is going to pay just that much less for his wheat. I say that the Transcontinental could have 5 p.m. taken the wheat from Estevan or any other point along the line at the rate of 6 cents a bushel that the minister has spoken of as being the rate from Armstrong to Montreal or Quebec-roughly speaking, a distance of 1,000 miles-and could have carried it at that rate to St. John. It could certainly carry it at a cheaper rate than the Canadian Pacific railway by lake and rail; therefore, there is no reason why the farmer in the West should be soaked 10 cents a bushel towards the close of navigation, simply because he is not sure of being able to get his wheat out. If the Government had had the necessary equipment and facilities for carrying the grain to St. John and Halifax, the farmers would have got 10 cents a bushel more for their wheat. After all this amount has been put into the railway, apparently hon. gentlemen opposite do not seem anxious to give the railway a fair show. If the Government had been desirous of doing
the right thing by the Transcontinental they would have provided the necessary equipment, the rolling stock, and the necessary facilities at tide-water, so that the grain could have been taken at any time of the [DOT]year down to St. John or Halifax at the rate the minister gave last winter for the
1,000	miles. The wheat could have been loaded into the ships there and the farmers would have saved a large amount on the price of their wheat. It would have added easily 10 per cent to the price they got. Every body from the West knows that towards the close of navigation the price of wheat goes down to cover the expense of keeping it during the winter. Here was a road built for the purpose of relieving matters, and well suited for the work; and if it had had the necessary equipment and technical facilities it could have handled the wheat to the advantage of the whole country, not only giving the farmers a much better price for their wheat, but enabling the road to earn interest on its cost.
With regard to the wheat that was commandeered I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce could have bought wheat after the close of navigation at considerably less than the Fort William price. The wheat could have been hauled over the Transcontinental to tide-water, and shipped to whatever point it was destined for; and in that way, either the purchasers would have got the wheat for a lower price or the farmers in the West would have got a higher price; and the railway, built by the country at a large expense, would have had an opportunity of doing the very thing for which it was built, and of earning interest on the money that had been put into it.

Is the minister going to tell the House how this rate ef six cents a bushel, from Armstrong to Montreal or Quebec, or ten cents a hundred, which is the same thing, was going to relieve the situation so much? We are all very much in the dark how it could relieve it. The point is that the rate to the seaboard from Quebec, which in winter is of course ice-bound, was more than as much again as the rate from Armstrong, although the distance was not half as much as the distance from Armstrong to Quebec. The Government owns two sets of rails-the new Transcontinental and the old Intercolonial-and has every facility for giving a cheaper rate. If they were sipcere-and I am not saying they were not-in their desire to get this wheat to a place of export, the minister should

tell us why they did not put in a cheap rate for export purposes. This rate to Quebec was a joke so far as export purposes were concerned.

I explained that a few minutes ago. In the summer season the Grand Trunk" and the 'Canadian Pacific railway companies have a certain rate between Winnipeg and St. John and Halifax. The lowest rate of the whole year is the rate during the summer season.. What was done by the Minister of Railways and Canals was this: he estimated the rate between Winnipeg and Armstrong, which is at a point equal to Port Arthur or Fort William. Then between Armstrong and Montreal he put into force a six-cent rate, so that the farmers in the West would have during the winter season the advantage of the lowest rate they could get on any railway for ,lake-and-rail transportation during the summer season.
Where did the grain go in, the winter time?

The hon. member knows that the terminus of the Canadian Pacific railway is St. John, and that during the winter time the Canadian Pacific Railway Company charges a much higher rate from Winnipeg to St. John than it does in the summer. The reason for that is that there is lake-and-rail transportation during the summer.
There is no rate to St. John in the summer?

There is to Montreal, and there is a rate to St. John in the winter. The farmers of the West had the advantage of the summer rate between Winnipeg and Montreal, and from Montreal to St. John they had the Canadian Pacific railway rate.
What advantage did they have by using this combination, rate over what they had by using the Canadian Pacific rate 'before .your rate went into effect?

When the elevators at Port Arthur and Fort William were filled the farmers of the West had to leave their grain either in their storehouses, or in the fields, or ship it over the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian Northern railway from Winnipeg to St. John, or to Portland, and if they shipped it over the Canadian Pacific railway they had to pay the winter rate. By shipping the grain over the Grand

Trunk Pacific and the Transcontinental they had the advantage of the summer rate between Winnipeg and Montreal.
What advantage did they receive by sending it to Montreal?

They could send it on to St. John or any other winter port at the summer rate. Suppose a farmer had a thousand bushels of wheat to ship from Winnipeg If he shipped it over the Canadian Pacific railway to St. John or to Portland, he would pay a high rate, because the Canadian Pacific rate is higher in the winter than in the summer. If he shipped it over the Government railways, he would get the advantage of the summer rate between Armstrong and Montreal; and the rate over the Canadian Pacific railway or the Government railway between Montreal and St. John is the same. The Transcontinental relieved the congestion in the West to the extent of
8,000,000 bushels. Hon. members complain that we did not ship out more. They say that we should have been ready to transport millions upon millions of bushels from the West. I have explained several times that we took over this road on the 1st of July; the Grand Trunk Pacific operated it for a month or two until we could get some engines and cars from the Intercolonial, but we robbed the Intercolonial of cars and engines in order to operate the Transcontinental as well as we did during the past winter. Hon. members know that it is an absolute impossibility to have engines and cars manufactured in a few days; they know that it takes several months to get equipment. We are trying to get it as quickly as possible, but a large number of cars and engines are necessary to operate a thousand miles of railway between Winni-[DOT] peg and Moncton. This winter I was very sorry that we had to take seventy-five engines and a thousand cars from the Intercolonial in order to operate the Transcontinental; because if we had had those engines and cars on the Intercolonial, we would have moved a very much larger quantity of freight between Montreal and St. John, and Halifax during the winter.
You leased a number of engines?

We leased twelve or thirteen engines from the Canadian Pacific railway and one or two from the Bangor and Aroostook railway. We did everything possible to get more engines. We had no equipment of any kind to start with, and I. think we did very well with the equipment

that we were able to put on the Transcontinental.
I do not say that there is very much profit in the eix-cent rate between Armstrong and Quebec, but it pays with a trainload such as I have stated. The Transcontinental has to be operated during the whole year, and in the summer months not very much freight is carried over this railway owing to the 'lake-and-rail transportation. When I say that the eix-cent rate paid, I mean that it paid a small amount over the operation of the train.
During this year we are going to buy more engines and cars, .so that when, the crop is harvested, we shall be able to carry a very much larger quantity of grain than we did last year. It is only along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific that we can assist in relieving congestion, because there is enough grain along that line to keep us busy.

The minister has admitted that about a thousand ears and seventy-five engines have been taken from the Intercolonial to operate the Transcontinental. What steps does he propose taking to restore that equipment to the Intercolonial? A great many complaints have been received at Moncton of the inefficient service rendered by the Intercolonial during the past year. Lumbermen, cattlemen, stock dealers, and mining corporations have been complaining that they could not get cars. The passenger . service during the past eight months or so has been almost disgraceful, the engines being wheezy, broken-down affairs, worse than the horses sold in Kings county to the Militia Department; in fact, those horses were Arabian steeds compared with the engines on the Intercolonial. There has been scarcely a passenger train that has not been two or three or four hours late, and the general complaint through the Maritime Provinces is that the service has been very bad. The reason was not apparent then, but it is apparent now: The Intercolonial was robbed in order that the Transcontinental might be operated. I do not think that is fair. The people of the Maritime Provinces have a right to receive as good treatment as they have been accustomed to receive in years gone by. The Intercolonial is a Government road and the service should not be impaired in the manner it has been. The minister must have known, when he was taking over the Grand Trunk Pacific, that he would require cars and engines, and it is altogether nonsense to say that it is impossible to procure cars and engines. Had he taken the precaution he would have had no difficulty in getting them; there are many car-building establishments in the country who would have been only too glad to be employed at any time within the last two or three [DOT]years. I would like to ask if he has taken any steps to restore the efficiency of the Intercolonial-which was none too good before?

I think it would be better that the question that has already been referred to, the reduction of rate from Armstrong to Montreal, should be more fully dealt with before we go into other matters. I do not know whether the minister can say now what the rate was from Armstrong to Montreal before the reduction was made. As I understand the situation, we are paying the same rate exactly from Winnipeg to Armstrong that we paid before, that is, six cents a bushel; and, as I understand further, we are paying the same rate from Montreal to St. John that we paid before. I am not trying to support the Government in not making a greater reduction, but I wish to be fair, as no doubt they wish to be fair. If the rate from Winnipeg to Armstrong is the same as it was before, and if the rate from Montreal to St. John is the same as it was before, and if the rate between Armstrong and Montreal has been very much reduced, then certainly there must have been a reduction on the whole.
No, for this reason: The freight rate to St. John is not made up by the addition of these three rates, but it is a through export rate.
Has the through rate from Montreal to St. John been added to? Is it more than it was before the Government undertook to make this reduction?

It will cost a person
more now to the seaboard if he uses these rates over parts of the route, and also uses the local rate from Armstrong to Quebec.

I understood that
the rate ^vas the same as it had been from Winnipeg to Armstrong and the rate was the same as it had been from Montreal to St. John. If, then, the Government made a reduction over a thousand miles of rail haul, there must have been a benefit to the farmers Of the West.

Undoubtedly, there was a large reduction. There is a through rate between Winnipeg and! Montreal, which obtains now in the summer season. In the winter time the grain has to go over the railway right through to Portland, St. John, or Halifax, and on that there is a through rate. But the rate on the Canadian Pacific was higher than it was on the Transcontinental and Government railways through to St. John or,-if it went over the Grand Trunk-to Portland.
Would the minister give us the rate?
I cannot give it offhand.

Does the minister have
this in mind-that owing to there being no elevator accommodation at St. John, there was no way by which the grain could be shipped from that port unless it came from the east side of the Intercolonial terminus, across to the docks on the west side? Does not he know that that would have to be added to the freight on grain coming over the Transcontinental to St. John? It would be very interesting to know what rate was actually paid from Winnipeg to West St. John by Transcontinental and the Intercolonial. I think he will find that the rate is the same as the rate by the Canadian Pacific railway.
The same to a cent.
No.

The minister is in
error. The rate was lowered for a stretch in the middle of the haul. But to seek to take advantage of tfiat would yield no advantage to the shipper. If an exporter had 10,000 bushels of grain, and decided that he would take advantage of that low rate from Armstrong to Montreal or Quebec, and then were to pay the local rate from Winnipeg to Armstrong and the local rate from Quebec to salt water, he would be out several cents a bushel.

As compared with the rate
between Winnipeg and iSt. John on the Canadian Pacific?

As contrasted with the
through rate to St. John, either by the Canadian Pacific or by the Grand Trunk. If the minister were to go into the shipping office of the Government railway in Winnipeg and then were to visit the shipping office of the Canadian Pacific, he would be

quoted the same figures to a cent and even a decimal of a cent. The rate is 33| cents per hundred or 201 cents a bushel. Unfortunately, the minister does not know the figures, nor have I the figures by me; but the late Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) and I have gone into this carefully, and we ascertained clearly that if a shipper were to try to take advantage of 'this lower rate he would be money out of pocket on the haul over the whole route. This is the one thing that the minister's department pretended to do for the farmers-and I do not use the word "pretended" offensively. Now, when we try to ascertain what it really means, a remarkable thing is that neither the acting minister nor the bevy of officers attending him on the floor, can tell us the through rate. One would have thought that this would be the one thing that they would have been able to state. Of course, I am not here to criticise the officers; it may not be reasonable to expect them to have this information or they would have had it.
I will get it.

And I hope the minister will find out how much grain went to St. John from the West and how much to Halifax, and what he paid. And would he ascertain whether the amount so paid was arrived at by taking account of the rate of six cents a bushel from Armstrong to Quebec, or was a through export rate obtained from Winnipeg, or from whatever point the wheat started from, to salt water? I am sure that not one of the minister's officials will tell him that the through rate from the prairies to salt water was one cent a bushel less over his railway than over the Canadian Pacific The minister talks about the summer rate to Quebec or Montreal. But what is the good of that on wheat that is going through in the middle of winter?-you might as (well tell the shipper that his bill of lading is of a pretty colour. The story we get from the Government is that the Allies want our wheat, and we are anxious that they should get it. But the Government do not in fact promote this trade. We have Government internal storage elevators that we cannot get filled. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) has the wisdom not to get into this discussion though the matter relates in part to his department. When the announcement was made that this benign Government-and I think a great deal of the Government in some respects-would make this concession for the

benefit of the farmers, naturally the farmers were greatly pleased. But when they came to bake advantage of it, they found that they had been acting under a misapprehension and that the change would not benefit them by a single cent; the figure is the same by the two railways, and there is absolutely no reduction.
A gold brick.

I did not say that,
though I confess the word was in my mind; but I do not wish to talk party politics in this matter. It was a gold brick that did not do anybody any harm. But, on the other hand, it did not do them any good, because it was soon found out. But there is this criticism that we have to make-if they can carry the wheat from Armstrong to Quebec at six cents a bushel and make money, or even pay expenses, it is a crime for them to charge eight and a fraction cents per bushel from Quebec to salt water. Because in doing this they are charging about one-third more for a haul of only half the distance. There is a nigger in the fence somewhere.
They either did not want thie farmer to get the good price, or they did not want to make this new railway a success. They are no 'fools in the Railway Department. They knew when they put that rate on that the stuff would not go to' the salt water; they did not want to see it go through and ma/ke a booming business over that railway. Why did they not establish just as good a rate on the Intercolonial, instead of maintaining a rate that is more than double? If they can afford to carry grain at that rate through that new country in Northern Ontario and Quebec there is no excuse for charging a rate doubly as high from. Quebec to St. John ' and Halifax. These are points that I would like the minister to look into and to inform himself upon.

Hon. gentlemen on the other aid!: are difficult to please. I suppose the Minister of Railways had not the least idea that he would be called upon to operate the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, which was not taken over, I understand, until the first of July of last year. That road was built by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and was supposed to be operated by them; yet hon. gentlemen on the other side have been calling the Minister of Railways to book because four years ago he did not start to provide rolling stock for the Grand Trunk 194
Pacific railway. Is that quite a fair thing to do? 'Surely not. Again, when the Minister of Railways tried to alleviate the situation-and my hon. friends from the West know it to have been serious-in the interests of the Western farmer, by taking from the Intercolonial railway what the Intercolonial could ill spare, a number of engines and a large number of cars, and sent them to do that Western duty for the Western farmer, then came forward a member from Nova Scotia declaring that it was a crime against nature and the Maritime Provinces that seventy-five engines, or any number of engines and cars, should be taken from the Intercolonial railway, which, to the infinite disgust and discontent and) confusion of Maritime Province dwellers, was left with only wheezy consumptives. He had not the heart to allow the Western farmer to get a single bit of solace or comfort; he and his own home must be looked after, no matter what became of the farmer's wheat. That shows the infinite difficulty of pleasing everybody. I am sure my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Railways will take a little comfort from the fact that he has steered the right course. The member for Moosejaw (Mr. Knowles) contends that no good has been done to the western farmer by the moving of 8,000,000 bushels of wheat out by this line during a portion of the winter. I think that this has been bene-ncial to the western farmer.
I did not say that it had not been beneficial; I said that the western farmer did not get the grain to the salt water any cheaper.

Throughout the country west of Winnipeg and west of Saskatoon there was insufficient storage for the farmers' grain, and quantities of it were lying in a more or less exposed condition, and therefore liable to injury. The elevators became' filled with grain, and storage could not be' extended. This
8,000,000 bushels of grain was so much extracted from the storage capacity of the West, which left a vacancy for 8,000,000 bushels to be salved and put into that storage. My hon. friend says that that did no good to the western farmer unless he got his grain into the consumer's hands; getting it down to Quebec and Montreal was of no use to the farmer of the West and did not make his position any better. I think my hon. friend is wrong in that. The grain got down at a summer rate to the elevators



of Quebec and Montreal. No greater storage charge was paid in those elevators than would have been paid, I imagine, in the western storage position. The western farmer got this 8,000,000 bushels down at a summer rail rate, partly into storage and partly perhaps into ships. This grain was taken to eastern ports and placed in storage, thus relieving the storage capacity in the West and allowing grain which other- ' wise would not have had storage to get storage there, and it was a relief to ^ the situation to that extent. My hon. friend stated that this road should have been thoroughly equipped, and should have begun to draw the grain out immediately after the crop had been gathered in the West. Well, little of it would go out by that route until the season of lake navigation was at an end. When the lake seaison is at an end and that line of outrgo is closed, then the railways take hold of it and carry it as best they can. If my hon. friend had got out 8,000,000 or 18,000,000 or 30,000,000 bushels by the last of October, or the middle of November at the latest, not one bushel of it -would have got any the quicker into the hands of the European consumer, simply because there was not the ocean tonnage to carry it. I think we ought to take that into consideration. Every bushel of wheat that was necessary and called for to fill the tonnage which it was possible to bring to the Atlantic ports, whether in Canada or not, was answerable to that call. That more did not go, that more co-uld not go, was due to the fact that there was not the tonnage to take -it away. The commandeered grain has been passing out through the Atlantic ports from the middle and later port of December until the present time, and there never was a moment when more grain was not waiting for the transports than there were transports to take it. What is true of that grain is true of grain generally, and would have been true of all grain that might have been brought out by that route or by any other route to Atlantic ports, whether Canadian or more southern Atlantic ports. Even if equipment had been available and the grain had been carried, it would not have passed into the hands of the ultimate purchaser and consumer in European countries any quicker. Whatever* was carried did get the advantage of being close to the seaboard and of having got there at a summer rate; moreover, it will be ready when navigation opens in the summer, and further tonnage comes to take it away.

Taking all these things into consideration I think that the congestion in the West was materially alleviated by bringing out these 8,000,000 bushels of grain, thus giving place to grain which would otherwise be dfeprived of storage.

I do not object at all to my hon. friend trying to defend the Government for its want of foresight, for its failure to equip the Transcontinental road. He and his colleagues have to make the best case possible, and I am quite content to leave their action or inaction to be judged -by the public. But I do complain of the reference which my hon. friend made to the remarks of the hon. member for Antigonish (Mr. Chisholm). I think he rather twisted that hon. gentleman's remarks and gave them a meaning which they did not bear. What that hon. gentleman meant, as I understood him, was that instead of waiting until they had to get rolling stock for the Transcontinental and robbing the Intercolonial railway of its proper equipment, the -Government should have taken time by the forelock and provided a proper equipment for the Transcontinental. That is what I understood the hon. member for Antigonish to say. Was that not reasonable? This Government, under the Act for the building of the Transcontinental railway, is given the power to operate various sections of the road pending its completion, and pending the time when the -Grand Trunk Pacific would be required to enter into the 50-year lease for that portion of the road. This Government ought, I think, to have done one of two things when they came into office nearly five years ago. It should have made up its mind whether it was going to operate the road pending its entire completion, or whether it should enter into an arrangement with the Grand Trunk Pacific to operate it. I have already called the attention of my hon, friend, but with very little effect apparently, to a statement which was made two, or perhaps three, years ago to the Minister of Railways in this House that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company had offered to take over the road as the various sections were completed, pending the completion of the entire line; that they had offered to thoroughly equip the road with rolling stock to the satisfaction of this Government, and to operate it under the direction of the Government, and subject to examination by the accountants of the Government. They offered to hand over any profits

of operation to the treasury of the country, and all they stipulated for was that, if there should be any loss in the operation of the road, that loss should be added to the cost of the Transcontinental upon which they would be called upon to pay interest at the rate of three per cent.
I want the committee to remember that the Minister of Railways promised distinctly and positively to take the matter up with the present president of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, and that he stated that he would inform this House of the result. But' from that day to this, so far as appears from the statement of the acting Minister of Railways, this Government has made no effort whatever in that direction. Therefore, what was the obligation resting upon it? The obligation was that it should provide the equipment and get ready for the operation of this line of railway. That was their duty to the great producers of the West, and their duty to the people o'f the whole Dominion in whose interests this great undertaking was entered upon. But this Government does nothing, although, as I have said, it has been in power now for nearly five years. Having apparently made up its mind that it was going to operate the road; having done everything it could do to prevent the Grand Trunk Pacific from entering upon its operation, a,tid having disregarded the contract and the specifications, thus rendering it not only possible but reasonable for the Grand Trunk Pacific to delay entering upon its operation, the obligation was on this Government. Did they not know what the railway was built for? My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke as if he thought it was a great thing, as if the Government was entitled to infinite credit, because
8,000,000 bushels of wheat had been carried over the Transcontinental. What was the road built for but to carry grain and all kinds of products? It seems to me that far from being entitled to any credit for carrying such a small amount of grain, for the small equipment it had, and for the poor facilities it provided, it should be condemned because it did not make the necessary arrangements and get the necessary equipment. Did the Government not know that one of the grand ideas which was put forward in connection with the Transcontinental was that it was to give a cheap rate in the winter, so that wheat and other products could be carried in winter as well as in summer, and in summer as well as in winter. That was the object in getting 194}	8
the low grades; that was the object in building a splendid roadbed; that was the object in going to very large expense to build the road to a very high standard instead of building it to a secondary standard. Yet we find that though this Government had apparently for a long time made up its mind that it was going to operate this road, it was absolutely without equipment, absolutely unprepared to transport the products of the West to the markets of the old world.
My hon. friend the Minister of Trade and Commerce says that there was as much wheat carried as could be carried, because vessels' were not available. Here again, we find a want of foresight. Ought not this Government to have foreseen, when the war broke out, that there would be transportation difficulties? Should it not have thought that vessels would be needed? Should it not have given some attention to the question of providing a Canadian merchant marine to meet the deficiency in vessels which has taken place. Hot one step did it take to meet the transportation difficulty, and to-day, after twenty months of war, with the ships of the Empire disappearing from the ocean in too great numbers for the comfort of the people of Canada and of the Empire generally, we are in the same state of lethargy; at least, this' Govern ment is as before. Not a thing has been done; not a thing is being done to provide proper transportation, and the only excuse the Minister of Trade and Commerce makes for hauling a paltry quantity of 8,000,000 bushels of grain over the Transcontinental railway, is that, even if more had been hauled, it could not have been transported to the markets of the old world. That is the excuse for not building the elevator at St. John to replace the one that was burned; that is the excuse for not enlarging the elevator at Halifax; that is the excuse for not providing any elevator accommodation at the port of Quebec. Does the Minister of Trade and Commerce know that at the port of Buffalo there is elevator accommodation for 50,000,000 bushels of grain? The grain of the West is brought there and stored preparatory to being sent over the American railroads to Baltimore, New York, Philadelphia and transported to the markets of the old world. In this country, we have spent millions upon millions of dollars on this great transportation system, and yet the only elevator accommodation we have in Eastern Canada is that provided by the small elevator at the port of Halifax, with a capacity of

750,000	bushels. After being in office for nearby five years, that is all this Government has to show: our ships declining, no effort at shipbuilding, our elevators burned down, and no steps taken to rebuild them. The elevators which were burned down having demonstrated that they were not sufficient even for the traffic of the Intercolonial, and still less for the traffic over this great Transcontinental system, no effort has been made to enlarge them, and no effort has been made to give adequate elevator accommodation at Quebec, St. John, Halifax or any other port on the Atlantic coast. The pitiable excuse that the Minister of Trade and Commerce gives is that, while it is true that we brought but a little grain, we brought little because we did not have the equipment in the way of locomotives and cars, that even if we had brought more we had no elevator accommodation, that if we had brought it to the sea coast we had no ships to transport it; so that altogether, we have been obliged to allow millions upon millions of bushels of grain to remain rotting on the prairies of the West and we have hundreds and thousands of our farmers reduced to a state almost of poverty with thousands of bushels of grain, gathered after laborious toil, for which they can get no return. That is the condition in which our western country has been left. The minister has made his apology but I do not think it is an apology which will satisfy this House or the people of the country.

I would like to ask the acting Minister of Railways and Canals a question. Grain can be hauled from Armstrong to Quebec, a distance of 932 miles, at a profit for 6 cents a bushel. The mileage from Winnipeg to Armstrong and from Quebec to St. John is 961 miles. Thus, two end pieces between Winnipeg and St. John have a mileage of 961 miles and the centre piece, from Armstrong to Quebec, a mileage of 932 miles, so that these portions are practically equal. In the discussion that has taken place in regard to the railway rates over the Transcontinental which were put in force some time last winter, no reason has yet been given why there was a difference in the rate per mile between that section of the line from Armstrong to Quebec and that section from Quebec to St. John.
The conclusion to which we are driven is that the rate was left as it was left so that it should not be, in fact, a competitive rate to an open winter port. The rate to St. John over the Transcontinental was identical with the rate over the Canadian Pacific, and the difference in the rates for the intermediate sections of the line only made the difference (mentioned by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster): It gave the benefit of storage capacity at eastern points instead of the capacity that would be needed to keep that grain stored in the West. Not to discuss these points at any greater

length, let me place before the committee the question in its general aspect. It appears to me to be of very much greater general importance than those who have spoken, on the Government side at any rate, seemed willing to accord it. If there is one thing upon which the future *welfare-the immediate as well as the distant future welfare-of Canada depends more than upon any other, it is the increase of Western production. That, I think, goes without argument. We are today faced with the statement, made on good authority, that, instead of production in the prairie country being likely to increase during the season upon which we are now entering, the area of production will be decreased as compared with last year. Some estimates are as high as twenty per cent decrease, some only fifteen per cent; but I have not seen any estimate less than fifteen per cent. That, at a time when the country and the Empire and the world may reasonably be expected to need increased production on the part of our western prairies, is a most serious consideration. It is not for lack of industry, nor is it for lack of enterprise, nor lack of opportunity, that the productive area is in prospect of decreasing this season as compared with last. We had, last year, besides a maximum area of production, a phen-omental crop. The result was an abundant return such as we have never seen before and such as," I am afraid, we need not expect again at any short interval. Had it been possible for the producers to realize upon that crop promptly and at the value that the demand in the world's market gave it, it would beyond any doubt have produced a condition of prosperity amongst the men actually engaged in production in the West and would have put them in a position to increase their production during the coming .season. I am aware that there are difficulties in the way of increasing production this year that did not exist last year. But the great thing that stands in the way is that many of those who were successful beyond their expectations in pro- [DOT] ducing last year have not been able to realize upon that production in time to put them in funds to go on with their enterprise this year. If I spent my money and my credit in producing an enormous crop last year, and have not been able to pay the debts I incurred in that production, I am not in a position to make extra exertions to produce a similar abundance during this coming year. It is not a question of whether I have the will or not, I have not the ability; I cannot do it, no matter how much I may want to do it. And I need not say to the House that, if I have been disappointed, as thousands of our people have been, in not being able to dispose of my crop under satisfactory conditions, I 'have not the heart, evpn if I have the ability to go on and make those exertions during the current year that must be made if the great results that we hoped for and that we need are to be achieved.
Until this present year, after the close of navigation on the lakes, it was not possible-or it was not reckoned to be possible-to bring grain forward to the seaboard. The western market was bottled up for a period of five months and was subject to such fluctuations of world prices and world conditions as might occur in the meantime. The result of that was, as was explained by my hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff), that every fall between the date of the harvesting of the crop and the date of the closing of navigation on the lakes-unless the crop was a partial failure-there was what was called a grain blockade, a condition of congestion caused by the farmer's desire to get hi,s grain out before the close of navigation, thereby saving the cost of storage and the extra cost of hauling during the winter months. Obviously, the grain that did not go forward before the close of navigation had to be held until navigation opened in the spring, at the cost of storage, interest, insurance, and possible unfavourable market fluctuations. The consequence was that there was a premium on grain that could be got forward and a discount on grain that could not be got forward. As I have said, this occurred yeaT after year; it was a necessary result of the conditions of the country whenever there was a large crop. Each year that condition of congestion meant tremendous loss to a large proportion of the producers of the West. I had the honour of drawing the attention of the Government of the day to that condition in 1911-a condition which resulted in tremendous losses during that year. It was believed that the construction of the Transcontinental railway over the shortest possible route, with the lowest possible grades and with the best possible construction, would not only increase the possibilities of traffic throughout the Dominion of Canada, but also eliminate-wipe off the slate absolutely-this condition of recurring

congestion or grain blockade. It was believed that this could be accomplished by creating a condition under which grain could be sent forward from the prairies to ocean ports all the year round at a favourable rate of freight. That was the purpose of the building of the Transcontinental railway; it was thought wise and prudent and economical to spend millions, tens of millions, even hundreds of millions, in the construction of that line in order to achieve that result. As the country increased in production, there was a corresponding increase from year to year in the disabilities resulting from the stoppage of the eastward flow of grain on the close of navigation. The time came when that road was completed. The last rail was laid in December, I think, of 1913, and in the session of over a year ago the Minister of Railways declared that the road was completed. It was stated-and the matter has been discussed since in the House-that there was a difference of opinion between the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and the Government as to whether the road was completed or not, the railway company holding that it was not completed, and that, therefore, they were not required to take it over; the Government holding that it was completed and that the railway company were defaulting when they did not take it over. Briefly, that was the condition a year ago; the last rail had been laid in the winter of 1913 and the Government in the session of 1915 declared that the road was absolutely com, pleted and was entitled to carry traffic to the full, and that the railway company that refused to take it over was actually in default. Following on the heels of that condition of over a year ago came the greatest crop that our country ever saw; oame the greatest prices for that crop in the market of ultimate consumption that we have seen in a lifetime; came the greatest demand for the crop that our country had ever seen.
