crop now, and shall be harvesting it in September, in about five months. Are we to believe that we shall not be able to dispose of that 150,000,000 bushels between now and next harvest? That is the conclusion we are bound to draw from what the minister has said. He speaks, no doubt, from information, and if his conclusion is correct the condition is much more serious than I had contemplated. We cannot have it both ways; we cannot have increased production and increased wealth, and, at the same time, a decreased market. If we cannot get the market, we cannot sell the stuff, and we need not' produce it. I quite bow to the minister's argument and to his information, but to my mind he has proved too much. I cannot accept his argument for the reason that I do not want to. I say frankly that I cannot bring myself to believe that that is our position, namely, that we have grain on hand that we cannot get rid of between now and next harvest. If this our position it is very serious. However well entrenched my hon, friend may be, I am going to take the contrary position and maintain that we have not yet overstocked the world, and that there are means, or we ought to find means, to bring to market the produce that we have available.

1 If my hon. friend is in that position and feels badly about it, I had better administer a little solace to lighten his mind, and not allow him to go up against the dead conclusion that I did not come to, and do
9 p.m. not wish him to come to, that there is no hope for the coming crop because the intervening surplus cannot be got rid of in the meantime. My whole argument has been directed to what my hon. friend started out with, namely, the realization within two or three months of the value at world rates of that 150,000,000 bushels which is now in the West, so that the blood current could come back and vivify the veins of the West, find start them in to the work of the present season. I say-and I maintain it because I believe it to be actually true-that as much wheat has been carried as could possibly have been carried if there had been 2o0,000,Uoa bushels more waiting at sea-board during

that intervening time. Now there are certain conditions which lighten the matter. In the scarcity oif tonnage, the distance that a boat travels is of importance, and if it is possible for a boat by travelling a shorter distance to make two or three voyages where otherwise she should make only one, and carry exactly the same cargo, that is so much in favour of the nearer country which has produce to sell. In that respect Canada has a great advantage;, it lies on the main tracks of ocean commerce and trade, where the vast majority of the world's vessels are going to and fro, and its distance from European centres is 2,500,
3,000	or 3,500 miles. In that respect Canada and the United States, in comparison with the Argentine, another large producer, and especially in comparison with Australia, which has been a very large producer this year, have the advantage of the shorter distance. Now, tonnage is growing scarcer every day. Do not let us deceive ourselves. Tonage is scarcer to-day than it was yesterday, and will be scarcer to-morrow; it will be scarcer next month than it is this month; it wili be scarcer day after day and month after month till this war ceases. It is impossible, however much you may desire or pray or objurgate, to get Tid of that condition of things. Now, Sir, what happened? The Australian Government undertook by Governmental intervention to procure all the surplus wheat of Australia, and became the sole charterer of vessels to take that surplus to Great Britain. She made advances to the farmers upon their grain with that idea.
But what has become of it? Where you have to make an 8,000-mile voyage to Australia for a cargo of grain the difficulties become greater than where you have to make but a 3,000-mile voyage across the ocean in order to get an equal cargo of grain'. To-day the tonnage is not going to Australia, and the necessities of the wheat market in the old country will be met, first of all, by those countries that are closest to it and that have the reservoirs of wheat.
Another advantage that Canada has over the United States is this, that the Canadian wheat of last season was, on the average, infinitely better in quality than the American wheat, and whilst some of the American wheat, by virtue of its poorer quality and lower price, is going in certain directions, those who want the best wheat are coming to Canada for it, and are finding it in Canada. Therefore, in the next few months, when the supply has to be largely
kept up , there is an opportunity for Canada to dispose of her surplus and to get her shelves cleared before they are filled again by the coming crop.
Canada was, during the past winter, in exactly the same position in which she will be during the coming summer.

I am not quite able to follow my hion. friend. In the first speech with which he favoured the committee he said that if you take the full capacity of the railroad, running ten trains a day, it can take out only 500,000 bushels per day, and it is going to take 300 days to transport the wheat o.f whichl my hon. friend speaks.
Not going to, 'but would take.
That is the same thing. A thing that will take is going to take.
Now we have water carriage.

My hon. friend the member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) rebuked the Minister of Trade and Commerce for presenting such a dark picture, saying that it was very discouraging for the farmers of the West if they would still have last year's crop on their hands when the crop of this year was harvested. Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce said: "Oh, in the next two months the farmers will be able to get last year's crop cleaned up." The two statements strike me as exceedingly inconsistent. What is the use of speaking about the enormous advantage Canada possesses by reason of the better quality of her grain, by reason of her nearness to the markets of the Old Country, if this Government does not take steps to provide requisite transportation facilities, both on land and on the sea, and also the requisite storage facilities? You may have all the advantages of a fertile soil and of excellent grain; but unless the farmers can get the grain properly taken care of and cheaply transported to the markets of the-world, all the natural advantages will be of no avail.
Do you suggest that the Government should go into the shipbuilding industry?

I do indeed. It almost makes one shudder to have the Minister of Trade and Commerce tell us to-night: "Ocean tonnage is scarce torday; it will be

scarcer next month; it will be still scarcer the -month after; it has been growing scarcer since the war began." Yet up to this, I think the twenty-first month of the war, this Government has taken no steps whatever to increase the ocean tonnage of Canada. Is not that fact enough to make one shudder?
Do not shudder.
I cannot help it. My hon. friend may think it is a light matter-
You do not.
It is a serious matter for the people of this country; it is a serious matter for the -farmer out on the Western prairie, who works there day after day from sunrise to sundown putting in his crop-
That is not the time he works; he works before sunrise and after sundown.

-suffering all the hardships of the lonely life on the prairie, to find, after he has harvested his great cron, that, owing to his not being able to g*t his grain to the market, it is rotting in the fields and he is losing thousands upon thousands of dollars. That is not an exceptional case. There are hundreds of pc pie who are in exactly that position. The minister speaks of ten trains a day. Let me tell him that he will find many railnads on the continent of America which are hauling twenty trainloads a day.
With a double track.

No, with a single track. It is the easiest thing in the world for a railroad to run twenty trains a day on- a single track. There would be no difficulty at all for a railroad with a track like that of the Transcontinental to run twenty trains a day, and, instead of 500,000 bushels, a million bushels could be taken out a day. With the three great railroads in the western provinces, properly equipped, you could take out 3,000,000 bushels a day, so that in sixty days you could take out
180,000,000 bushels of grain. What did this Government do? According to the showing of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, they hauled out during the past winter what with ten trains a day could be hauled out in sixteen days. That is the extent of the wonderful assistance which the Government have been trying to make the people believe they were giving the farmers of the West.

Unless we have transportation on the ocean, the Government can get all the-grain to the seaboard and yet have accomplished only half its purpose; if the Government does not have proper storage facilities in its elevators, it can only half assist in the-proper development of the West; and I do not see how any one can disagree with me when I say that the Government in respect of these matters has wholly fallen down. What does the Minister of Trade and Commerce say to the fact that, at the great port of St. John, which was the first port to take-a forward step to divert the traffic from Portland in the state of Maine to Canadian seaports and through Canadian channels, and which has developed the winter-port trade very rapidly during the past twenty years, although the elevator connected with the Government railway system was burned down over two years ago, this Government, has not yet replaced it? What does he say to the fact that the only storage in connection with the Government system of railways, including the Transcontinental, is the one small grain elevator at Halifax, with a capacity of 750,000 bushels? What does he say to the fact that 80 per cent, of the grain of the Canadian West has gone this year through American ports? What does he say to the fact that at least 60 per cent of that grain is housed in the elevators at Buffalo, if my information is correct?
It is not correct.
What percentage has gone through there?
A little over 50 per cent- nearly 60 per cent all told.
That, is getting pretty close to 60 per cent.
You said 80 per cent.

The attention of this
Government has been called to the absolute necessity of having storage facilities east of the Great Lakes and on the Atlantic coast. Sir William Van Horne, over and over again, spoke of the necessity of carrying out this policy. Yet, as I have said, notwithstanding that these facts were brought to the notice of the Government, no step whatever has been taken to increase the elevator capacity in the East. If the Transcontinental had been properly equipped with rolling stock, or if the Government had handed that road over to the Grand Trunk Pacific on the 'terms on which it had been arranged by the late Government that they should take it over in sections as completed,

it would have 'been able to haul, not eight million bushels but forty or fifty million bushels, and that without the slightest difficulty. Then if the Government had provided storage capacity, grain could have been stored at Quebec, Montreal, St. John and Halifax, and, as the ships were available from time to time, it could have been sent forward to the markets of the world. If the Government had taken the steps that I think they ought to have taken, and that I beg them to take even at this late date, to send our grain forward to the markets of the world, the problem will ibe nearer to a solution than it is. The situation to-day is not by any means a satisfactory one. The Government ought to give thought to the question, instead of treating it lightly, and laughing and jeering at the suggestions made for improvement and development. Even though the thoughts I express may not be of the loftiest character, they might bring their great minds down to the practical, and endeavour to settle this question, to the very great advantage of the people of Canada.

My hon. friend has asked me three questions, and I am quite willing to answer them. It may be that then he will not shudder so frequently and so obviously as he has been doing when reciting this terible condition of things. The statement is made that there is not	sufficient	storage at	St. John,Halifax and Quebec. I just want to say	this-and the	hon.	gentleman
knows that what I have to say is true -that, as far as relieving the situation this year is concerned, any additional storage which could reasonably have been provided in St. John,' Halifax and Quebec, would not have made one iota of difference as regards the quantity of grain actually delivered in Europe from Canada-not one iota. In this Dominion of Canada, there is elevator storage for about 150,000,000 to
165,000,000 bushels of grain. It is not a good argument, it is not reasonable, to say that you must have all this storage, or indeed a majority of this storage, at the seaports themselves. The all-year seaports on our Atlantic coast are not the places where the big storage capacity is provided, or where it is best to provide it. These ports are for transfer (purposes, not for storage purposes. In order to transfer quickly and well you .must have a certain storage capacity in proportion to the vessels that come there seeking
for loads. But you do not need more storage capacity than this, and it is better to have your grain stored in the interior than at the ports themselves, it is less costly and less burdensome to the port itself and in every way better for the distribution of the grain. Now, it will not be pretended that for transfer purposes it would have been necessary to provide at St. John additional storage for more than
2,000,000 to 3,000,000 bushels. If you had had that all these months since the close of navigation, you would not have shipped one bushel more out of St. John than actually has been shipped, because there never has been a time when a vessel came for a cargo of grain and the grain was not there for it. The reason why more was not shipped is that it was not possible to get tonnage for it. The commandeered grain that has been passing out from this country since the last of December and up to the-present time, and which will not all be out probably until the middle of May, has been carried under transport conditions-directed by the Governments of Great Britain, Italy and France. And Great Britain, Italy and France, those powerful Governments, have not been able to provide more ships for that commandeered grain than there was commandeered grain at the seaports ready to put into the vessel.
Was the commandeered' grain going to Italy or to England?
To Italy mainly, a portion of it to France, and a portion to-Great Britain.
But the bulk of it to-Italy?

Yes, and when that is cleared out of the way, the bulk of it will go somewhere else unless Italy wants more, a-s she probably will. You are up against certain conditions, and it is foolish, it is no argument at all, to say that any particular individual or any particular government is responsible for these conditions. The greatest problem these nations have to solve to-day is the problem of tonnage for the supply of the army and of the people, but particularly for the supply of the army. You are up against a condition which neither the 'Canadian 'Government, nor any other government in the world, is able to cope with successfully. We have simply to live out these conditions and make the best we possibly can of them; and it is assertion and only assertion, for

my hon. friend to say that the Government is responsible for an insufficiency of tonnage at these ports to carry the grain of the Northwest. The Government is not responsible for it, and no government, however powerful it might have been, could have made better headway than this Government has made against the conditions which have existed for the last twelve months.

If to do nothing is to make progress, then the Government has been exceedingly successful; for it has done -and I defy contradiction-absolutely nothing since this war broke out for the encouragement of shipbuilding in Canada, or the establishment of a Canadian merchant marine. It has done nothing in any direction whatever. The minister says that tonnage has become scarcer month by month-
Does the hon. gentleman seriously suggest that vessels could have been built since the war began?

With proper encouragement we could have had some steel ships completed. We could also have had-I am told on good authority, at leasi^-two hundred wooden vessels built, each with a capacity of from four to five thousand tons, and equipped with auxiliary motive power so that it could make a trip across the Atlantic in about double the time occupied by an ordinary tramp steamer. These vessels would have been of enormous benefit. In the United States they are being built and used with very great success. It is hardly necessary to say that this would have relieved the stringency of the situation enormously. In a conversation that I had with him, Mr. McNdchol, for a long time general manager of the Canadian Pacific railway, spoke of the very great necessity of having large storage capacity east of the Great Lakes. In Buffalo, as I have said, they have a storage capacity of about 50,000,000 bushels. What would be the difference between the desirability of storage at Buffalo or east of the Great Lakes and that of having it at ports on the St. Lawrence, or the Atlantic? The idea that elevators upon the seacoast are intended for transfer purposes proceeds upon the assumption that vessels would be constantly coming to take away the grain as it arrived by train. Would it not, therefore, be just as desirable to have large storage capacity at the seacoast as it is to have it east of the Great Lakes?

I could! not follow the argument of the Minister of Trade and Commerce when he suggested that within the next few months the position in regard to ocean transport was going to improve. Canada is to-day geographically situated where it was a year ago; whatever advantage we ever will have we have had during the past winter. If it is a fact-and there . is no doubt thlat it is-that tonnage is getting scarcer from day to day, our position will be that much worse during the months to come than it was during the months that have passed. I see no relief for the situation that confronts us. through the facts placed before us by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. With regard to elevator capacity, the hon. minister says that it is not necessary to have elevators at ocean ports. Well, our greatest ocean port is Montreal, and we have a very large elevator there.

My hon. friend must not put it in a manner more extreme than I did. I did not say that it was not necessary to have storage facilities at ocean ports. What I meant to say was that ocean ports are chiefly for transfer purposes, but that a reasonable amount of storage is absolutely a safety and an assurance even at transfer stations.

I would think it is absolutely a fact that there is a necessity for elevator capacity, even storage capacity, in some degree, at an ocean port. In fact; the Government is building an elevator at Vancouver, having that point in view. The Government, therefore, is stripped of any justification for not having adequate elevator facilities at St. John, Halifax and Quebec. Since this Government has been in power it has built three very fine interior elevators in the Prairie West which until the present time have found no serious usefulness. It would have been just as competent for them to have built at the ocean ports the elevators that they put up at Moosejaw, Saskatoon and Calgary. With all due respect, I think they would have served a more useful purpose at these ocean ports.

I do not think
that.	.

My hon. friend knows
that until the last two or three months these elevators had not served any purpose at all.
Why did the farmers not use these elevators more?

Because they were not
needed.
Why not?

Because they were not;
that is all. Why should a man pay for hauling grain to an interior elevator and have it remain there if he could <ret the grain forwarded to the ocean port?
I thought they could get their money, or a large part of it. if they got their grain to these interior elevators?

If they could forward to
an ocean or lake port just as well, certainly they were going to do it. The only possible usefulness of these interior elevators would be in the case of an unfavourable season, when it would be necessary to have the grain dried - in this . case their drying plants would be useful-and where there was a prospective congestion or blockade at the closb of navigation, in which case the railroads would have a short haul to the interior elevator instead of going down to Fort William. But with an open road all the year round to the Atlantic ports, that condition did not and should not arise-as a matter of fact, would not arise if the lines to the Atlantic ports were operated as it was intended that they should be operated. There could not be any fall congestion, because the conditions in the fall would not give rise to it.

Then it was not a
good policy to build these elevators?

There is no doubt that
until within the last two or three months the money spent upon these elevators was thrown away, for they were not used. Conditions might arise through unfavourable seasons which might cause the elevators to be very useful. They are being used now, but the reason they are being used is because the grain is not being carried forward to the ocean ports. We have the trackage facilities, but apparently we have not the rolling stock, or we have not the intent or desire to send the grain forward. The hon. minister contends that if we got it forward we could not ship it. Well, if we had it forward we would have that much of the work done, and be in that much better position to ship it when the opportunity arrives. However, the serious point is this:
if circumstances were such during the past six months as absolutely to prevent our grain from goipg forward across the ocean, unless conditions-if conditions are blam-able-do not become very much more favourable than they have been in the past we are not going to be able to get rid of what we have before our next harvest comes on. That is a very unfortunate condition, and again I say that I decline to accept the position of the hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce on that point.

I think we all agree that
at the ocean ports we should have quite a lot of elevator capacity. Of course, we 'must have, and will require as soon as we can arrange it, larger storage capacity at St. John and Halifax, but the fact of our having such a large storage capacity in Montreal, which, no doubt will be increased from time to time, assists us so far as the ports of St. John and Halifax in the winter are concerned, because we can store large quantities of grain at Montreal, and then in the winter move it to St. John and Halifax. I shall be in a position at another sitting to give more information with reference to the rate question that we discussed this afternoon.. I stated that I did not know what the arrangements were when this rate was made by the minister himself, but I have made some inquiries since the matter was brbught up. To-morrow I shall take it up with the general freight agent of the Intercolonial and be able to give more details. As I understand it, the advantage of that arrangement was this:
In the summer, the rate is 6 cents per bushel from Fort William to Montreal. In the winter time, over the Canadian Pacific Railway and, I presume over the Canadian Northern railway [DOT] too, the rate is 12 cents per bushel from Fort William to Montreal. The rate say from Winnipeg to Fort William is 10 cents per 100 pounds. The advantage was this: any farmer shipping, say, from Fort William to Montreal over the Canadian Pacific railway would pay 12 cents per bushel in the winter time, and 6 cents from Winnipeg, say, to Fort William. That would be 18 cents. Over the Trans-' continental he would pay 6 cents per bushel to Armstrong and 6 cents per bushel to Montreal or Quebec, so that the farmer shipping from the West on the Canadian Pacific railway or the Canadian Northern at their regular winter rates would pay 18 cents per bushel from Winnipeg to Montreal or Quebec while over the Transconti-



nental he would pay 12 cents, thus saving 6 cents per bushel.

What is the rate from
Montreal to St. John by the Intercolonial, compared with the rate from Montreal to St. John by the Canadian Pacific railway?

The rates we are talking
about are through rates.

Is it not true that while the Government has lowered the rate on a portion of the line, the total through rate on the Government system of railways from Winnipeg to St. John is not less than the rate on the Canadian Pacific railway.
The rate is, as I have said, lower by 6 cents per bushel.

For what distance?
Mr: REID:	I have just explained that
the through rate on the other roads to St. John would be 6 cents per bushel more.

Let us have this matter understood. Does the minister state positively that the rate on the Government system of railways from Winnipeg to St. John is 6 cents per bushel less than the rate on the Canadian Pacific railway?
What I said was-
That is what the minister said.
Let me answer the question in my own way.

We want to have this
cleared up. 'We say that the Government has simply made a pretense of lowering the rate for a short distance. What I ask the minister is-it is a plain question, if he will pardon me-will he state that the rate on grain during the past winter from Winnipeg to St. John over the Government system of railways was 6 cents per bushel less than the rate on the Canadian Pacific railway.

If the hon. member will allow me, I will answer that question, in my own way. In the first place, I said that if he would wait until to-morrow, until I could get the information, I would be able to answer.
That is better, but the minister pretended to answer.

I did not give any definite answer, so far ae that was concerned. I said that grain that was shipped on the Transcontinental to Montreal and Quebec for export-some of it is in store in Mon-
treal and Quebec, and some went to Portland, the Grand Trunk having taken it to their terminal-that grain shipped for export to Quebec, Montreal, or Portland over the Transcontinental road was carried at a rate which was 6 cents per bushel less than , would have been charged if it had been carried over the Canadian Pacific railway to Montreal or Quebec for export.

The Canadian Pacific
Railway has no line to Portland.

We are talking about grain for export, and that is the information I have at the present time, that the rate over the Transcontinental is 6 cents per bushel less than the rate on the other roads. There was not any grain shipped to St. John because we have no way of storing it there. We could not take it over the Transcontinental and deliver it without putting it into the Canadian Pacific Railway elevator, there, and the hon. member knows that the Canadian Pacific Railway elevators at St. John were taxed to their utmost capacity this year by the grain which that company hauled over its own railway system.
I understood my hon. friend to say that some went to St. John and Halifax. He says now that none went to Halifax or St. John, but that al'l went to Portland.

Some 400,000 bushels of the
8,000,000 bushels went to Halifax. There are one and three quarter million bushels stored at Quebec, and there is a large quantity in store for export at Montreal waiting for the opening of navigation. But a large portion went to Portland; I cannot give the quantities.

The minister must see the importance of it. There must be a through rate on the Government system of railways from Winnipeg to St. John and Halifax, because St. John and Halifax are two large exporting ports. Will the minister say that the through rate on grain for export during the past winter was 6 cents per bushel less on the Government system of railways to Canadian Atlantic ports than bn the Canadian Pacific Railway?
I must admit again that I am not fully seized of the facts this evening, but I will get the hon. member that information. He could not expect me to have that information this evening.

I thought the minister would have it. He is making a great handle of the reduction of 6 cents on a part of the line between Armstrong and Quebec. In the winter season the great question is, what is the through rate for export to the Atlantic ports, and that is why I should have thought that the minister would have the information.

Is it not the fact that the Government decided to fix that 6 cent rate from Armstrong to Montreal after consultation with the other companies, and was it not practically understood that the other roads, the Canadian Northern and the Canadian Pacific Railway, would give practically the same rates?

My information is that there was no consultation, that the other roads did not give that rate, and that it was in operation only on the Transcontinental. The Minister of Railways took the responsibility of making that rate himself for this reason: we had in Montreal a very large storage capacity, and he thought that if we could fill the elevators there-I do not know the exact capacity, it may be anything from 8,000,000 to 10,000,000 or 20,000,000 bushels-that if, also, we could fill the elevator at Quebec, which has a capacity of
1,500,000	bushels, the farmers of the West would get the advantage if they paid the same rate that they would have to pay in the summer by shipping it to Port Arthur, lake and rail. They would not ship their grain in the winter time if they could possibly avoid it, because it would cost them the winter rates on the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern, which would be 6 cents more than if it were carried on the Transcontinental. As I understand it, that was the reason which actuated the Minister of Railways. He said, we have the elevators at Fort William and Port Arthur filled, and we have in Montreal a considerable storage capacity. If we can carry the grain over the Transcontinental, and put it in the elevators at Montreal and Quebec, where there is a capacity of one and three-quarter million bushels, and the farmers can get it carried there at the same rate as they would pay in the summer time, it will be of great assistance to the people in the West.
The only reason why we could not handle more was that we had not the equipment. We took the road over on the first of July with the expectation that wre would get our proportion of equipment that the Grand Trunk Pacific was supposed to have on
195J
hand for the Transcontinental, but, on the contrary, we got none. We took that road over without a particle of rolling stock. We did the best we could bytaking rolling stock from the Government railway system. We have ordered rolling stock, but it will be eight or ten months before it is delivered-. You cannot get cars for months and months after the order is given on account of the scarcity of raw material. During the last year or two the policy of railway companies has been to 'build steel, instead of wooden, cars, and it is difficult to get the material. However, the minister did order cars-, we are ordering more, and we are doing our best to get sufficient equipment to meet all the necessities of the road. Taking the condition as we found it, it does strike me that it is not bad work that has been done by the Minister of Railways since the road was taken over. We hope we will get the road as well equipped as the Intercolonial was- at the time we took the Transcontinental over, and that we will have it 'in- such shape that we can move the grain in larger quantities and avoid the trouble we had with grain being exposed last winter. If we can get the necessary equipment, with the great storage capacity we have at the head of the lakes, at Montreal, in the West, where three elevators were built last year, at Quebec and -in Ontario, where the elevator capacity has been increased very materially within the last few years, and with, the elevator capacity that we must -have at St. John and Halifax, I think we will be able to handle the -crop fairly well. This is a big question and one which requires a great deal of consideration, and will call for considerable expenditure. At St. John, where the elevator is supposed to be built out on the point near the sugar refinery, tracks will have to be laid and other work done. I admit that there has been quite a delay in the building of that elevator.
Quite an inexcusable delay.

I do not agree with the hon. gentleman in so far as that is concerned.
I agree that it is necessary to have the elevator there, and as soon as possible. But war cpnditions have been such that many works o.f great importance, such as the one mentioned, has had to wait.
The Minister of Finance said that all necessary works that could not be called new would be carried through to completion.
I have had this matter up and I am in hopes that it will only be a short time until we have an elevator in St. John.

I should like some one to put in a word for the building up of Canadian industries. I have heard of nothing but wheat. We cannot eat wheat, nobody -can eat wheat, but we all eat flour. We could reduce our elevator capacity, and the facilities for moving wheat, by half, by turning the wheat into flour. But, we allow the industry, flourmaking, in Great Britain and elsewhere to be built up at our expense while we are trying to get our rajw product transported across the ocCan and carried elsewhere. Why is it that some method cannot be devised, why is not the impulse to manufacture strong enough in this country, why do we not repress this tendency to freedom of trade, which is so absurd, and why is it that we never think of developing our own country? Let us bend all our energies towards turning our wheat into first-class flour, and then try to send that elsewhere, and not keep calling for enormous storage capacities half of which, as a matter of fact, would not be required, if we had our ideas properly developed in regard to our own industries, and in regard to giving the people of this country something to do, and we would be saved that expense, which in itself is tremendous.

I am afraid that my hon. friend is wrong. He often is right, but I think he will have to go a step further. We do not eat flour; we eat bread and biscuits, and he will have to carry his argument down to the manufacture of the flour into bread and biscuits if he is going to carry his idea out to its logical conclusion. I was almost going to say that he had done it more effectively than it was done on this side of the House. The Acting Minister of Railways and Canals rather discounted that by arguing that the Government had done a great deal by transferring a lot of it to Montreal and Quebec. I think the Acting Minister of Railways was right in saying that that was a good idea; but I am not so sure that he was quite right in saying 
that they had carried that idea into practical effect. The minister's figures must surely be wrong. I cannot conceive of a statement that only 400,000 bushels, out of
8,000,000 bushels, went to a Canadian port.
No, I did not say "went to a Canadian port."
To Halifax.
I should have added in winter. I should have added to a winter port. You said that 400,000 went to Halifax and none to St. John.
No.

A great deal of it went to Portland. I cannot see how my hon. friend, having a Government line from the West, did not even fill the elevator at Halifax once. He tells us that we ought to have more storage capacity at Halifax; yet, out of the 8,000,000 bushels, he did not ship
750,000	to Halifax. That rather bears out something that was said in the discussion the other night, and which was that the way the railway has been managed has made it practically imperative that a large portion of our western wheat should be carried to an American port. The road has been operated in a practical way to Cochrane, but east of that as a side line, a local road, and not with any regularity. An excuse was given why proper operation has not taken place. The result has been, just what the minister has said to-night, that a large proportion of the 8,000,000 bushels that came from the West over that road has been handed: to the Grand Trunk at Cochrane. The Grand Trunk has brought it out over the Toronto and Northern Ontario to North Bay, from there over its own line to Scotia Junction, then east to Montreal, and from Montreal to Portland. Now, until the Government takes hold of this line east of Cochrane, and gives it a service at least approximating the services west of Cochrane, the result cannot be otherwise than that' in winter a large proportion of our western wheat will go to American ports. That is altogether subversive of the policy behind the construction of this line. The Grand Trunk cannot begin to haul as big a load over its line from North Bay to Montreal as can the Transcontinental from Cochrane to Moncton; there is no question about that. I am safe in saying that the Government railway from Cochrane to Moncton, with no more than two short pusher grades, can haul in one train twice as heavy a load as can be hauled over the Grand Trunk from Scotia

Junction east. If the Grand Trunk can afford to take that traffic from Cochrane to North Bay, and from there to Scotia Junction, thence to Montreal, and from Montreal to Portland, over a comparatively inferior line, surely the Government line with its magnificent roadbed ought to be able to haul the grain to our Canadian ports at a cheaper rate. I am suprised that only
400.000	bushels got to Halifax. If there was no tonnage to be had, the Government should at least have filled up the Halifax elevator out of that 8,000,000 bushels.

The hon. member knows from many discussions we have had in this House that the Intercolonial has been taxed to its utmost capacity from the close of navigation up to the present time, carrying troops and waT supplies, and there have been complaints throughout the whole system because we could not furnish cars for local traffic. The Intercolonial could not have done more than it did during the last season. The grain was stored in the elevators, at Montreal and Quebec, and how could we take it to St. John or Halifax when we had not the power or the cars?

It struck me that as
400.000	'bushels had been taken to Halifax, the elevator there might have been filled. It would have taken only about 350,000 bushels more to fill it.
It was not stored there; it only went through the elevator.

There was no tonnage
there. '

Yes, there was tonnage, but not a very great deal. I say the Intercolonial was taxed to its utmost capacity, and could not have hauled that 8,000,000 bushels. But give the Government a chance to get equipment for both roads, and then the grain will be moved over the Government railways to the elevators at Montreal and Quebec, and to the ocean ports. Grain has to have some outlet. The
10 p.m. Canadian Pacific railway was taxed to its utmost capacity at St. John, and as the grain had to be shipped to England we could not help it going through American ports.
Is this item of $1,500,000 for equipment for the Transcontinental?

No. I have a memorandum here showing that the $1,500,000 is made up as follows:
Filling wooden trestles, $350,000; fencing, etc., etc., $100,000; unsettled grading contracts, $500,000; right of way and Quebec terminals, $500,000; boilers and power house equipment, Leonard shops, $50,000.	There are three
trestles on the line just west of Superior Junction, (that is, the 10 miles of line constructed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company and subsequently acquired by the Transcontinental Commission) that it may be advisable to fill this coming summer.	They were constructed in 1908, and must now be either renewed or filled. There are other wooden trestles between Graham and Winnipeg that were constructed in 1907 and 1908, that it .may be advisable to at least partially fill up this coming summer. It costs considerable money to organize equipment for trestle filling, and it is a question, when once organized and at work, whether it is not more profitable to complete the job at once. I am of opinion that $360,000 will be sufficient for this class oif work between Superior Junction and Winnipeg for the season of 1916. As all trestles on the line east of Superior Junction are of more recent date than those west of that point, they should not be filled for some years to come.
Considerable fencing will be required between Hervey Junction and La Tuque, a distance of 50 miles, as the country is settleing up. The same applies to the country east and west of Cochrane and the country adjacent to the Wabi-goon river west of Graham, but it is possible that the above-mentioned amount will not be expended, as this will depend largely on whether the anticipated amount of settlement takes place or not.
The unsetted grading contracts amount to: Grand Trunk Railway Company, $1,500,000 ; unsettled contractors' claims, $203,000. The above is a matter of adjustment, and it is impassible to state definitely what the final result will be.
Many of these right-of-way questions in Quebec and vicinity are now in the Exchequer Court for adjustment. In other cases, they may be settled without having recourse to the courts. I am of opinion that the sum of $500,000 will be sufficient for the adjustment that will be affected within the fiscal year.

Surely the acting minister can see now what he has done. He has read some detailed items of construction, which show that the filling of trestles, fencing, etc., has not been comnleted Under the original contract the Grand Trunk Pacific was to be fenced. The minister admits the whole case about the road not being completed. However, we can discuss that on the Transcontinental item. Can the minister say how much of this
8,000,000 bushels went into the Quebec and Montreal elevators respectively?

I am informed that 6,250,000 bushels went to Montreal, and 1,750,000 bushels to Quebec. A portion of the grain that went to Montreal elevators has been shipped out to Portland, but we shall not know the exact quantity till spring.

I have always understood that steamships are very glad to get grain to use in place of ballast, and I know that some years ago vessels going to New York would carry grain just for the sake of having it as ballast. I should think that the ships coming to our Canadian ports in winter would be glad to get grain to store in the hold.
They got all the grain they wanted to carry.

The quantity of war supplies that had to be shipped was so great that nearly all the vessels had cargoes of that nature.
But they got all the grain that they wanted to make up their cargo, not as 'ballast but at very high rates. For years the rates for ballast have been very low; but, of course, owing to the scarcity of tonnage, there was such a congestion of freight that they could get nearly all the freight they wanted.
Is the Government taking steps to secure tonnage?

The question of securing tonnage does not come under the Railway Department. It comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce, and the next time that the Estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce are before the House, perhaps the minister will be able to reply to that question.

The minister has given us a great deal of information, but there is one point on which he has not thrown very much light. He has admitted that the scarcity of rolling stock on both the Intercolonial and the Transcontinental is a serious matter, and I know that the business people of the country are anxious about it. Would the minister be kind enough to take us into his confidence and tell us what he has done in regard to providing cars and engines?

There are quite a number of engines and cars under order. I gave instructions some time ago to have the specifications ready, and I expect within a few days that tenders will be called for for a very large .quantity of cars and engines and other equipment necessary. In order to help us out, we purchased the equipment of one of the contractors.

What contractor was
that?

O'Brien and McDougall. We purchased from them 25 engines, 400 cars,

and a quantity of other material-all the plant necessady for construction and keeping the railroad in repair.
It was pretty well worn out.

I am informed that it was in good condition. The 25 engines and 400 cars have come in very useful. We expect, however, to have under order within the next few weeks all the cars and engines that we can get made in this country between now and next fall.
Ordinary wooden cars or steel under-frames?
What we intended making was the steel cars, but we had in view the building of say 500 wooden cars to keep Us going, as we can get those much quicker than the steel cars.
Steel under-frame?
Yes. The reaeon that there was a shortage of rolling stock on the Intercolonial was, as I stated this afternoon, on account of our taking a quantity of equipment to put on the Transcontinental.
Would the minister mind bringing down a report showing what he purchased from O'Brien & MoDougall and what he paid? *
I will send my hon. friend a copy of the detailed account.

I hope the minister will not delay very much longer in getting his specifications out and calling for tenders, because it is slow work building steel cars. Every one knows that a sample car has to be .built, that the stock has to be procured ahead, and that it takes months to get started on a contract of that kind, because some of the large car plants in the country are busy on war material. I regret that the minister has let the whole winter pass without having his contracts entered into. If he really intends to get anything done that will serve us for the coming season, he should not be so far behind .as at the present time to be only calling for tenders.

I have been pressing this matter with those who .have to get the specifications out, and they tell me that within the next few days we shall be able to call for tenders, and we expect to get the first 500 cars in July.
Do you build any cars at Moncton?
We only do repairing work there.
You build some engines there?
Yes, but we have a contract for nearly all those outside. We do a little of that -work at Moncton.

Is there not sufficient capacity at Moncton, in those magnificent shops, 'which are well equipped and where you have the very best machinery? It was understood, when those shops were erected, that care would be built there.

As I stated a minute ago, those shops are being run to their fullest *capacity with repairs and so on. When the men are not employed on work of that kind they work at the building of oars. My information is that the shops at Moncton, owing to heavy repair work during the last year, are working to their fullest capacity. They are not holding off any work; all the work that can be done there is being done *at the present time, but it takes the whole plant to keep the equipment in order.

Is the minister quite certain that it is the scarcity of oars that has placed the Intercolonial in such a position that it is not able to take care of the traffic? It is inconveniencing the people very much.

That is the reason-because we had to take equipment from the Intercolonial to put on the Transcontinental between Winnipeg and Quebec, as at the start we had no ears at all on the Transcontinental. Had we not had to do that we would have been in a much, better position on the Intercolonial.

It is the opinion of some people in the Maritime Provinces who have some knowledge of the matter that it is not entirely the scarcity of cars that is bringing about- this unfavourable condition, but that it is to some extent due to the management. To illustrate this point, in Halifax [DOT]on Saturday last a wholesale merchant informed me that on the 8th of April a loaded car for him left Montreal and on the 23rd of April he could not find any trace of it.

That is easily explained. There have been cases on the Intercolonial, as well as on other roads, of local freight having had to be put on a siding or in the yards and kept there for days in order to allow the through traffic for the war to go
forward. Ammunition and supplies foT war purposes had to have the right of way.
There is another reason that just strikes me as to why there was a little shortage. The hon. member who comes from Prin'ce Edward Island will remember that there was some trouble because goods could not be shipped to Newfoundland. We had 300 cars at Sydney, where they were held for months because the steamers running from Sydney to Newfoundland could not take the freight. We had to place an embargo on freight for Newfoundland because the steamers could not take it across. We had to send a Government steamer, the Durley Chune, to carry two cargoes, in an effort to relieve the situation. We chartered another steamer also. All that time there were cars held up. But there were other places where we had to let cars wait. This has been an exceptional time-we all admit that. We had to use many engines in moving the troops. A troop train, being very heavy, would require two engines, and the hon. gentleman knows how many troops have been moved. That has meant taking power from the moving of freight. Besides *all this, we have had to take over the Transcontinental, making it very hard to meet all requirements. I think the management has done everything possible under the circumstances.

Here was this car leaving Montreal on the 8th of April, routed for Halifax, and loaded with stuff that the people were waiting for, inquiring about, [DOT] and ready to unload, but they could not even get information as to where it was. My information is that under the management of Mr. Pottinger the local men were able to give a good deal of information with regard to matters of that kind, but under the management of Mr. Gutelius nearly everything is done in Moncton. The statement is made that when you write to Moncton jiou do not even get an answer in any reasonable time. I know the conditions in Prince Edward Island. Under the former management tlqe local superintendent- had a great deal of responsibility and could give the information to the public, but now everything is transferred to Moncton and you might almost as well write to China as to Moncton, so far as getting an answer is concerned. The matter is referred from one official to another. The present management may be better in some respects that we cannot see. but it does not give the

same satisfaction to local patrons. The case to which I have referred is one that the former management would not have permitted to remain unsettled. I quite understand that a car may go astray on the railway, but surely it can be traced; at all events, a letter might be answered. A wholesale merchant in Halifax told me that this case was not an isolated one. but that similar cases often happen. There is a belief that the management is not trying to give the local people the service they have the right to expect.

Our general freight agent,
Mr. Hayes, is a man in whom I have a [DOT] great deal of confidence, and I am surprised to hear it said that there is such a feeling as the hon. gentleman speaks of.
I think it is on account of the trouble we have had this winter. But the Intercolonial is not the only road on which there have been delays. A case was brought to my attention of a complaint made of eight or ten cars that had been en route on a large system for three months and that they had not been able to locate-they had got run on to some siding, no doubt, and other freight had accumulated. Of course, even under normal conditions, cars will go astray. But from what I have known of the working of the Intercolonial during the present winter-and I have had a good deal to do with it because of the minister being away-I believe it has not been any worse in regard to delays than any other system.

Whatever
the reason, one thing is certain, and that is that there is general criticism of the management of the Intercolonial. That criticism is not confined to the officials and the employees. The minister, no doubt, knows the attitude of the employees towards the management at Moncton, he knows that ever since the change a few years ago there has been nothing of the spirit of cooperation and good will that prevailed among the employees. He knows that even newspapers supporting the Government criticise the management'. I refer particularly to a newspaper in Truro, in the constituency represented by the chief whip of the Conservative party (Mr. Stanfield), which, in season and out of season, criticises the Intercolonial management. Why it is I am not in a position to say. But we do know that there is a large staff, and the Lord knows they get good salaries, and the cost of running the service is altogether out of proportion to the cost of the 
service when Mr. Pottinger ran the road. Complaints are not confined to the operations of last winter, but have been general for a number of years past. There seems to be indifference on the part of the officials at Moncton to the requirements of the local trade. They seem to think they are the lords of creation and can do about as they like, and if they reply to a complaint they seem to think it an act of condescension on their part. The people along the line in Quebec and the Maritime Provinces complain bitterly about the lack of sympathy shown by the officials at Moncton. We regret that the Minister of Railways (Mr. Cochrane) has been prevented by illness from giving the attention to the service that he would have liked to have given.
Whether it is due to the fact that there are too many new men on the job, that the offices go from one man to another, and that the work is done in a perfunctory manner, I cannot say. The feeling prevails that there is very little sympathy on the part of the management, even on the part of the minister, with the railway and the people of the Maritime Provinces. Another matter that I wish to call attention to is the delay that occurs in dealing with small claims against the Intercolonial. When a small claim for a horse injured or sheep killed is sent into the department at Moncton, investigation after investigation is held; the matter goes from one man to another; the operations are even more mysterious than the Militia Department was beiore the war broke out. You call attention time after time to these little claims; after some time probably you get a reply, but the thing hangs fire. The delay in the Chancery case that Dickens describes-I cannot recollect the name of it-
Jarndyce and Jarndyce.

The delay in connection with that case was nothing compared with the tardiness of the Intercolonial Railway in dealing with these little claims. The minister ought to prod them up a little and see that these claims are promptly dealt with. It is all very well to say that the claimants may go to court about it, but the minister knows that in connection with these little claims running from $10 to $100 the claimants do not feel like running a risk of lawsuit with a powerful defendant like the Intercolonial Railway. I submit that in all fairness these claims should be promptly dealt with; that advantage should not be taken of technicalities. More time

and money is wasted in running these things from pillar to post than would be involved in settling the claims promptly.

I have not heard any complaints such as the hon. member mentions. We have a solicitor at Moncton who looks after these claims, and there is no reason why they should not be disposed of with reasonable promptness. I will draw attention to the statements the hon. member has made, and see that there is as little delay as possible in dealing with claims that may arise in the future.

There is a pretty general feeling that the officials who came from the Canadian Pacific railway, particularly those who were loaned, are not in sympathy with the Intercolonial. I do not know whether or not that iis correct, but if it is correct it is a serious state of affairs.

I do not think that is a
fact.

There is room for suspicion there. The system has been changed since the new management took hold. Under the management of David Pottinger, who received a small salary, comparatively speaking, there were two tariffs in each year-I think this applied to the Prince Edward Island railway as well as the Intercolonial railway-a summer tariff and a winter tariff. When the tariff went into operation in the spring, every one concerned knew what the tariff would be until the fall. Now the tariff is changed quite frequently, and nobody knows how often it is going to be changed. I have spoken to station agents along the line of the railway and they do not seem to know clearly what the tariff is. Many circulars are sent out in connection with these changes. A circular will go out referring, perhaps, to section 10 of circular 82, subsection g ox something like that, and it keeps a man reading pretty nearly all the time in order to be well posted with regard to the changes. The result is that a man frequently charges too much in order to uc safe. The idea is that the Intercolonial is tailing along after the Canadian Pacific railway. This session of Parliament a committee has given its attention to the matter of introducing the fish business into west-Canada. Mr. Archibald, superintendent of the dining car service on the Intercolonial railway, who appeared before that committee, was asked upon what principle they charged as much in the dining cars for fish that cost five cents a pound or less as for
turkey that cost from 20 to 25 cents a pound. The Government railway system could be made a good advertising agency.
Did he explain the reason?

He said he knew of no
reason unless it was that they wanted to copy the Canadian Pacific railway. There does not appear to be any originality or any responsibility in connection with this Toad; the only desire seems to be to copy the Canadian Pacific railway I understand that on the railway systems in the Southern States they make a specialty of putting fruit in the dining car at a very low rate in order to advertise the fruit districts. On the Hill system they make a specialty of certain kinds of potatoes that are grown in Oregon and in some of the Pacific coast states. It would be an excellent advertisement for our fish if the Government railway system should put fish on the menu card at as low a rate as possible. There is no doubt about the fact that the dining car service is good, but few men who are accustomed to eating fish will take fish if they can get turkey at the same price. I was coming up the other day on the Intercolonial and to my surprise I found that turkey could be obtained even at this season of the year as cheap as haddock. I took the haddock, which I found to be excellent. We are spending money in an effort to advertise the fish business and to introduce it into western Canada; why should the Intercolonial Railway not advertise it on theiT own tables? The only reason that is offered seems to be that they want to follow the lead of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
You have the Prince Edward Island oysters, I believe, on the bill of fare?

No, it is not the oyster
season.
I mean during the season.
I suppose they have them.
They are good, too, the very best in the world.

I think so. I see an item here for original construction on the Prince Edward Island railway. Surely that must be a misprint. If I understand the words " original construction," this item should surely be $8,000 or $18,000.

No; that is an item to cover any claims. The explanation of it is this: it is a revote of amount of unexpended bal-

a aces from the [DOT] 1915-16 appropriation. In 1915-16 we had a vote of $800; it remains the same. Each year there are Land damages and claims that have not been presented, or that have been overlooked, and, having a small appropriation, a settlement can easily be made at a reduced figure. There was not anything spent last year, and there is nothing in view, but it is just as well to have this small item in the Estimates in case anything should turn up.

Some years ago the Government built a piece of railway extending from a place called Cardigan to Montague, and the intention was to continue that line and connect with what is known as the Murray Harbour branch. That line has never been completed, and it ought to have been finished. The intention was to finish it, but, for some reason or another, it 'has not been completed. Now the war is on, and I suppose that will be another reason for not going on with it. The line between Cardigan and Montague was completed by the late Government, and the intention was to extend it so as to connect with the other branch and make it more useful than it is now.

These Estimates were prepared by the Minister of Railways himself, and he does not appear to have an item for that railway. I do not understand the situation or the conditions, but there is nothing in the Estimates, and, therefore, there would seem to be no intention of going on with that work this year.
There is an item of $1,000 for surveys and inspection. That has been in, the Estimates for a year or two, but it does not seem to have .been used.

During the past year the night of way surveys have been made on the island, under the vote for this purpose, to obtain records of the profile, right of way, bridges and so forth. The records will be completed this year, but it is necessary to revote the balance to complete the plans and records.

For two years the Minister of Railways told me that he intended to survey a proposed line of railway between Bridgetown and the main line, connecting probably at St. Peter, and passing through or near the settlement called Strathcona, but no survey has been made. Is it the intention to have (anything done this year?	.
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l

During the war we are not going on with any more new work than we can possibly help. There is no vote for that work.
iMr. HUGHES: There were surveys made last summer, were there not?
No, those were for the purpose of obtaining the records of profile, right of way, bridges, and so forth, on the island.

I saw a number of men making surveys there every time I travelled on the railway. They called themselves engineers, and they carried tripods and surveying instruments of various' kinds. I think they were having a pretty good holiday. They seemed to be young men from college, and a good many worked bareheaded, with their sleeves rolled up, and with their boots over their trousers, and there was a considerable quantify of mud on their boots. There was a local election coming on.
That accounts for it.
It was reported that the [DOT] survey was for the purpose of having the gauge of the Prince Edward Island railway widened.
That was probably right.
If that is correct, is it the intention of the Government to proceed at once with the widening of the gauge?
There is nothing in the Estimates for that purpose.
That is why I thought it strange that they should be making surveys last summer, if there was no intention to go on with the work.
The surveys have to be made ahead.
That may be so, but the opinion is that the coming election had something to do with it.
I do not think so.

It will be hard to get that idea out of the minds of the people down there, particularly when the surveys are not to be followed up by any work. If there had been an item in the Estimates showing that the survey was to be taken advantage of, and that the work was to go on, I might have thought that it was all right, but I must say I am somewhat skeptical. I am afraid that that

survey will have to be done all over again. A local election was held last summer, .and there was a .possibility of a Dominion election as well, and perhaps it was thought that the survey would do for both. It is one way of spending money, and of giving a holiday to young men who are sons or relatives; of men friendly to the Administration. It is not a desirable way of spending money, particularly when we ought to be practising economy. It is adopting the method which was suggested some sessions 'ago, that the Government should dash away and spend the money.

Will the minister get some information about this car ferry and give it to the committee, when the Estimates next come up? He might tell us how far we have got oni with it, and all about it. I would suggest that we let the Prince Edward Island item through.
Will the minister say when the car ferry will be ready for operation, or when the piers will be ready?
I discussed that matter with the officials a few days, ago, and I understand that the car ferry will be ready this coming fall.
Would it not be better for the minister to give us the information definitely?

I will get that information. We have had a very interesting and useful discussion to-day, and if the committee is willing to let this item go through; I would suggest that we rise and report progress.
Progress reported.
